248	### agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1
249	
250	(wink + agent, 2026-10-18, restructured 2026-10-20) Small rule fixes learned by running v0.3.0,
251	dead-end cycles defined, and the end of every rung and of Land reshaped, so that what the user
252	reviews is what is published. Follows **feat: vc-x1 commit, install, and run-dev**, whose commands
253	the rules below name. Each change is a `####` heading holding what is done, and its `#####` holds
254	why.
255	
256	#### Never rename
257	
258	- The package keeps its plain name throughout a cycle: Opening step 6 and Land step 1 go, and
259	  `versioning.md` Dev artifact name is rewritten around the `[install]` table and the dev root.
260	- Land step 4 becomes `vc-x1 build`, a `vc-x1 run -- -V` smoke check, and `vc-x1 install`.
261	- Fast and full then differ only by `-- --include-ignored`, the fourteen `dr1_*` tests, and are
262	  identical once **dr-1 is built in Rust** drops their `#[ignore]`. What fast becomes is decided
263	  then.
264	
265	##### Why: never rename
266	
267	The rename's restore at Land changes the closing after its review, by a squash into a pushed
268	commit, and Land step 4 names no command.
269	
270	#### A local commit pair before every push
271	
272	- Per-rung flow steps 8 and 9 merge, since `commit` pushes what it commits: on the description
273	  review's go, `vc-x1 commit -s b --title --body` makes the pair and publishes it. With `--no-push`,
274	  or `[commit] push = false`, it keeps the pair local for a look at the commit itself, description
275	  and diff together, by `vc-x1 show -s both @-` or gitk, and `vc-x1 push -s b` publishes it after.
276	  A fix is edited and folded by `vc-x1 squash -s b`, a description fix by `squash -s b --title
277	  --body`.
278	- A commit made by hand, a draft below `@` with no description, is described in place by `vc-x1
279	  commit -s b -r REV --title --body`, its trailer stamped and its partner made, never by `jj
280	  describe`, and `--bookmark` moves the cycle's bookmark onto it past any nearer one.
281	- Step 6's work review stays ahead of it.
282	- Committing vs pushing is rewritten, `vc-x1 commit` committing both repos, `squash` continuing
283	  a rung, and `vc-x1 push` publishing, and `jj.md`'s vc-x1 push section follows.
284	- Re-describing: the rule becomes never by hand and never on a published commit, since the pair
285	  carries trailers from the start and `squash --title --body` is the sanctioned re-describe.
286	
287	##### Why: a local commit pair
288	
289	The last closing's review came after its push, so a change meant a remote rewrite and a
290	squash-push in both repos. Made as a pair, both trailers are known at commit and push carries no
291	description, so the reviewed commit is the published one. The work review stays first so a
292	description is not rewritten while the work still moves.
293	
294	#### The scope flags in the rules
295	
296	- Every `vc-x1` invocation in the agent-files carries its scope: `sync -s b` at the sync points,
297	  `commit -s b`, `squash -s b`, `push -s b` in the per-rung flow, and `squash-push -s a` for the
298	  user's squash-push, replacing `--scope=both` and `-R <agent-dir>`.
299	- Every argument is a flag, no positional: `commit -r REV`, `push -r REV --bookmark NAME`, and
300	  `squash-push --bookmark NAME`. Step 9's `vc-x1 commit -s b --title --body`, At rest's `squash-push
301	  -s a`, and `jj.md`'s vc-x1 push section's opening were brought current in this copy by **feat:
302	  push, commit, and squash-push take flags only**, the invocations alone, the Committing vs pushing
303	  rewrite still this proposal's.
304	- The rest of the commands too, by **feat: the other commands take flags only**: `versioning.md`'s
305	  adoption names `agent-files copy --from` and `diff --from`, and `hooks.sh`'s guard test names
306	  `install --dev`, `build-dev`, `install-dev`, and `run-dev` being `build`, `install`, and `run`
307	  with `--dev` now. A rule that says `install-dev` says `install --dev`.
308	- And then by profile, by **feat: build, install, and run take --profile**: `--dev` retired to
309	  `--profile dev`, so `hooks.sh`'s guard test names `install --profile dev`, and a rule that says
310	  `install-dev` or `install --dev` says `install --profile dev`. The `[build]` and `[install]` keys a
311	  rule might name are `commands`, `dir`, and the `[profile.<name>]` tables.
312	
313	##### Why: the scope flags
314	
315	`-s` is required on the write commands and `sync` once **feat: vc-x1 commit, install, and run-dev**
316	lands, so the rules' invocations must carry it or fail.
317	
318	#### The closing is a trapezoid or linear, and converts
319	
320	- A multi-step cycle closes as a trapezoid by default or as linear on request, the closing commit
321	  carrying the shape, so nothing is reshaped at Land.
322	  - `vc-x1 commit --closing <BM|REV>`, naming the cycle's tip, onto the trunk, `--land`'s bookmark
323	    or `[cycle] trunk`, `main` when absent, makes the closing in the shape `--shape
324	    <trapezoid|linear>` names, else the `.vc-config.md` key `[cycle] closing-shape`, else
325	    trapezoid, and prints which decided.
326	  - Trapezoid is the merge of the trunk and the ladder's tip. Linear is a plain commit on the
327	    ladder, so the trunk carries one commit per rung, the shape the rules called keep separate,
328	    renamed.
329	  - The key is the project's preference, so each adopter sets its own, and one that sets nothing
330	    keeps the trapezoid.
331	  - Either converts to the other while the closing is a draft, before Land, by re-parenting the
332	    same closing: its change id, trailer, and, with the trunk unmoved, its tree are kept.
333	- Land is sync, then `commit --closing <BM|REV> --land [TRUNK]`, the fast-forward and the push,
334	  then `vc-x1 install`. To test the closing before it is published, it is made without `--land`,
335	  its release build, the candidate, installed off the PATH by `vc-x1 install --dir <DIR>` and
336	  tested by its path, and the candidate lands it, `<DIR>/vc-x1 land -s b --onto <TRUNK>`, and
337	  installs itself, `<DIR>/vc-x1 install`. The fast-forward lands the tree tested, so `cmp
338	  <DIR>/vc-x1` with the installed binary finds no difference, and the plain `vc-x1` is replaced
339	  only by what is on the trunk. The bookmark deleted is the one `--closing` names, or for a revision its
340	  current or nearest parent bookmark above the trunk, several refused with the list, and the
341	  branch's other bookmarks are left and named as merged. The trapezoid recipe goes,
342	  Close-out step 5 keeps the user's choice, the key its default, and carries it out by the flag,
343	  and `jj.md` Close-out shapes names the two shapes and why squash is not a shape.
344	
345	- The shape's name: with one rung the figure is a triangle, wink's observation (2026-10-20), so
346	  "trapezoid" names one case. The tool calls the operation `merge` and the result the merge
347	  close-out, and the rules' text could follow. `commit --closing` merges into the trunk as it is
348	  now, a bookmark read where it points, so a `main` that moved during the cycle no longer stops Land
349	  for a rebase. A linear closing cannot join a moved trunk without rewriting the reviewed ladder, so
350	  its Land refuses one.
351	
352	##### Why: a trapezoid by default, linear on request
353	
354	The trapezoid keeps every rung reachable while `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle,
355	and it joins a moved trunk. Some prefer a straight history, which linear gives, and the choice is
356	made at the closing, so the shape is in the commit that was reviewed rather than a reshape at Land
357	made after it. Converting is cheap while the closing is a draft, so the choice is never final
358	before Land.
359	
360	#### A cycle's shape is its branch's commit count
361	
362	- [Cycle shape](AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)'s "A ladder that shrinks to one rung still closes as a
363	  ladder" goes: a branch with one commit above the trunk, the opening alone, is a single-step cycle,
364	  and `commit --closing <BM|REV>` finalizes that commit in place, the bare cycle title replacing the
365	  opening's, while more commits get the closing commit. Every closing names its tip, by the cycle's
366	  bookmark or a revision, `@-` the common one, and the count reads the branch, so there is no bare
367	  form, and `--dead-end` always makes the closing commit.
368	- Any commit on any line closes: a tip that is not `@-` is closed by a detour, `@` moving onto it
369	  and returning after, and the commits above it stay as they are.
370	- A parent wrong after the fact is fixed with `vc-x1 reparent`, never by closing again.
371	- Every cycle starts with `commit --opening`, a single-step cycle included: its bookmark is created
372	  and pushed at the trunk, and its one commit begins as the opening, the work squashed into it. So
373	  Opening step 2, the bookmark's creation and publication by `jj git push`, is `commit --opening`'s,
374	  and the step names it.
375	- The closing's title and body may be left out: the cycle title is read from the opening, and the
376	  body comes from `.vc-config.md`'s `[closing] body`.
377	
378	##### Why: the commit count
379	
380	The tool tells the shapes apart by counting, with no title to read, and a cycle need not decide its
381	shape before its first commit: it is single-step until a second commit makes it a ladder.
382	
383	#### A commit body is two plain paragraphs
384	
385	- The problem, then the solution opening "Solution:", ending with the pointer to the record where
386	  it is at that commit, "See details in zDOING.md." on a rung and "See details in zCLOSED.md." on
387	  the closing, which moves it, no bullets, and the rung subsection the full account: the entry **A

reviews is what is published. Follows **feat: vc-x1 commit, install, and run-dev**, whose commands
the rules below name. Each change is a `####` heading holding what is done, and its `#####` holds
why.

#### Never rename

- The package keeps its plain name throughout a cycle: Opening step 6 and Land step 1 go, and
  `versioning.md` Dev artifact name is rewritten around the `[install]` table and the dev root.
- Land step 4 becomes `vc-x1 build`, a `vc-x1 run -- -V` smoke check, and `vc-x1 install`.
- Fast and full then differ only by `-- --include-ignored`, the fourteen `dr1_*` tests, and are
  identical once **dr-1 is built in Rust** drops their `#[ignore]`. What fast becomes is decided
  then.

##### Why: never rename

The rename's restore at Land changes the closing after its review, by a squash into a pushed
commit, and Land step 4 names no command.

#### A local commit pair before every push

- Per-rung flow steps 8 and 9 merge, since `commit` pushes what it commits: on the description
  review's go, `vc-x1 commit -s b --title --body` makes the pair and publishes it. With `--no-push`,
  or `[commit] push = false`, it keeps the pair local for a look at the commit itself, description
  and diff together, by `vc-x1 show -s both @-` or gitk, and `vc-x1 push -s b` publishes it after.
  A fix is edited and folded by `vc-x1 squash -s b`, a description fix by `squash -s b --title
  --body`.
- A commit made by hand, a draft below `@` with no description, is described in place by `vc-x1
  commit -s b -r REV --title --body`, its trailer stamped and its partner made, never by `jj
  describe`, and `--bookmark` moves the cycle's bookmark onto it past any nearer one.
- Step 6's work review stays ahead of it.
- Committing vs pushing is rewritten, `vc-x1 commit` committing both repos, `squash` continuing
  a rung, and `vc-x1 push` publishing, and `jj.md`'s vc-x1 push section follows.
- Re-describing: the rule becomes never by hand and never on a published commit, since the pair
  carries trailers from the start and `squash --title --body` is the sanctioned re-describe.

##### Why: a local commit pair

The last closing's review came after its push, so a change meant a remote rewrite and a
squash-push in both repos. Made as a pair, both trailers are known at commit and push carries no
description, so the reviewed commit is the published one. The work review stays first so a
description is not rewritten while the work still moves.

#### The scope flags in the rules

- Every `vc-x1` invocation in the agent-files carries its scope: `sync -s b` at the sync points,
  `commit -s b`, `squash -s b`, `push -s b` in the per-rung flow, and `squash-push -s a` for the
  user's squash-push, replacing `--scope=both` and `-R <agent-dir>`.
- Every argument is a flag, no positional: `commit -r REV`, `push -r REV --bookmark NAME`, and
  `squash-push --bookmark NAME`. Step 9's `vc-x1 commit -s b --title --body`, At rest's `squash-push
  -s a`, and `jj.md`'s vc-x1 push section's opening were brought current in this copy by **feat:
  push, commit, and squash-push take flags only**, the invocations alone, the Committing vs pushing
  rewrite still this proposal's.
- The rest of the commands too, by **feat: the other commands take flags only**: `versioning.md`'s
  adoption names `agent-files copy --from` and `diff --from`, and `hooks.sh`'s guard test names
  `install --dev`, `build-dev`, `install-dev`, and `run-dev` being `build`, `install`, and `run`
  with `--dev` now. A rule that says `install-dev` says `install --dev`.
- And then by profile, by **feat: build, install, and run take --profile**: `--dev` retired to
  `--profile dev`, so `hooks.sh`'s guard test names `install --profile dev`, and a rule that says
  `install-dev` or `install --dev` says `install --profile dev`. The `[build]` and `[install]` keys a
  rule might name are `commands`, `dir`, and the `[profile.<name>]` tables.

##### Why: the scope flags

`-s` is required on the write commands and `sync` once **feat: vc-x1 commit, install, and run-dev**
lands, so the rules' invocations must carry it or fail.

#### The closing is a trapezoid or linear, and converts

- A multi-step cycle closes as a trapezoid by default or as linear on request, the closing commit
  carrying the shape, so nothing is reshaped at Land.
  - `vc-x1 commit --closing <BM|REV>`, naming the cycle's tip, onto the trunk, `--land`'s bookmark
    or `[cycle] trunk`, `main` when absent, makes the closing in the shape `--shape
    <trapezoid|linear>` names, else the `.vc-config.md` key `[cycle] closing-shape`, else
    trapezoid, and prints which decided.
  - Trapezoid is the merge of the trunk and the ladder's tip. Linear is a plain commit on the
    ladder, so the trunk carries one commit per rung, the shape the rules called keep separate,
    renamed.
  - The key is the project's preference, so each adopter sets its own, and one that sets nothing
    keeps the trapezoid.
  - Either converts to the other while the closing is a draft, before Land, by re-parenting the
    same closing: its change id, trailer, and, with the trunk unmoved, its tree are kept.
- Land is sync, then `commit --closing <BM|REV> --land [TRUNK]`, the fast-forward and the push,
  then `vc-x1 install`. To test the closing before it is published, it is made without `--land`,
  its release build, the candidate, installed off the PATH by `vc-x1 install --dir <DIR>` and
  tested by its path, and the candidate lands it, `<DIR>/vc-x1 land -s b --onto <TRUNK>`, and
  installs itself, `<DIR>/vc-x1 install`. The fast-forward lands the tree tested, so `cmp
  <DIR>/vc-x1` with the installed binary finds no difference, and the plain `vc-x1` is replaced
  only by what is on the trunk. The bookmark deleted is the one `--closing` names, or for a revision its
  current or nearest parent bookmark above the trunk, several refused with the list, and the
  branch's other bookmarks are left and named as merged. The trapezoid recipe goes,
  Close-out step 5 keeps the user's choice, the key its default, and carries it out by the flag,
  and `jj.md` Close-out shapes names the two shapes and why squash is not a shape.

- The shape's name: with one rung the figure is a triangle, wink's observation (2026-10-20), so
  "trapezoid" names one case. The tool calls the operation `merge` and the result the merge
  close-out, and the rules' text could follow. `commit --closing` merges into the trunk as it is
  now, a bookmark read where it points, so a `main` that moved during the cycle no longer stops Land
  for a rebase. A linear closing cannot join a moved trunk without rewriting the reviewed ladder, so
  its Land refuses one.

##### Why: a trapezoid by default, linear on request

The trapezoid keeps every rung reachable while `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle,
and it joins a moved trunk. Some prefer a straight history, which linear gives, and the choice is
made at the closing, so the shape is in the commit that was reviewed rather than a reshape at Land
made after it. Converting is cheap while the closing is a draft, so the choice is never final
before Land.

#### A cycle's shape is its branch's commit count

- [Cycle shape](AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)'s "A ladder that shrinks to one rung still closes as a
  ladder" goes: a branch with one commit above the trunk, the opening alone, is a single-step cycle,
  and `commit --closing <BM|REV>` finalizes that commit in place, the bare cycle title replacing the
  opening's, while more commits get the closing commit. Every closing names its tip, by the cycle's
  bookmark or a revision, `@-` the common one, and the count reads the branch, so there is no bare
  form, and `--dead-end` always makes the closing commit.
- Any commit on any line closes: a tip that is not `@-` is closed by a detour, `@` moving onto it
  and returning after, and the commits above it stay as they are.
- A parent wrong after the fact is fixed with `vc-x1 reparent`, never by closing again.
- Every cycle starts with `commit --opening`, a single-step cycle included: its bookmark is created
  and pushed at the trunk, and its one commit begins as the opening, the work squashed into it. So
  Opening step 2, the bookmark's creation and publication by `jj git push`, is `commit --opening`'s,
  and the step names it.
- The closing's title and body may be left out: the cycle title is read from the opening, and the
  body comes from `.vc-config.md`'s `[closing] body`.

##### Why: the commit count

The tool tells the shapes apart by counting, with no title to read, and a cycle need not decide its
shape before its first commit: it is single-step until a second commit makes it a ladder.

#### A commit body is two plain paragraphs

- The problem, then the solution opening "Solution:", ending with the pointer to the record where
  it is at that commit, "See details in zDOING.md." on a rung and "See details in zCLOSED.md." on
  the closing, which moves it, no bullets, and the rung subsection the full account: the entry **A

#### A commit body is two plain paragraphs

- The problem, then the solution opening "Solution:", ending with the pointer to the record where
  it is at that commit, "See details in zDOING.md." on a rung and "See details in zCLOSED.md." on
  the closing, which moves it, no bullets, and the rung subsection the full account: the entry **A
  commit body is an intro and a pointer to the record** in `## Todo`, its rule, specimens, and
  subsection change. The bookends stay pointers, "Opens the cycle ..." and "Closes the cycle ...",
  with the same pointer after them.

##### Why: two paragraphs

A `git log` reader gets what was wrong and what was done in two sentences, and the breakdown is
written once, in the record, rather than twice.

#### Ladder labels from `[0]`

- `notes.md` and the `cycle-model.md` specimen number the ladder's reference labels from `[0]`.

##### Why: labels from zero

Each label then equals its rung's version suffix.

#### A rung may run the acceptance check

- Close-out step 1 says a rung may run it and the closing records the result.

##### Why: a rung may run it

Some checks run only mid-ladder, as in **fix: a missing fixture fails instead of passing**.

#### Dead-end cycles defined

- A cycle abandoned after its opening pushed still closes and lands. Its closing, titled with the
  cycle title plus " dead-end closing", keeps what is worth keeping, reverts the rest, and records
  what was tried, why it stopped, and what replaces it, then lands as a trapezoid like any closing.
- The title cap does not bind the suffix (wink, 2026-10-20).
- In `AGENTS.md` Close-out, `jj.md` Close-out shapes, and `prose.md`'s bookend titles.
- Open: whether a dead end's Land releases its bare version or reverts to the last release.
- First run: **test: the tests build the dr-1 fixture**, closed 2026-10-20.

##### Why: dead ends land

The cycle's agent-repo commits are on `main` and their `ochid:` trailers name its work-repo rungs,
so dropping the bookmark would leave them naming nothing, and landing keeps every rung reachable.

#### Warn rather than refuse

- Open, asked and unanswered (2026-10-24): wink's principle "warn rather than refuse", for a check
  whose failure may be a legitimate shape rather than a mistake, possibly a rule in
  `agent-data/code.md` beside the unwrap alert.
- Its uses so far, in `commit`: a title ending " closing" without `--closing` is warned about, a
  draft below `@-` and a closing with no bookmark are kept local with a line saying why, and a
  closing is never refused for an empty `@`.

##### Why: warn rather than refuse

We think a refusal of a legitimate shape sends the user to raw `jj`, which the tool exists to
retire, where a warning names what was done and leaves it reviewable before the push.

#### Continuation notes go in the closing

- Close-out step 7's notes are written before the closing commit, which carries them, so the
  work-repo is clean from the Land on and At rest's "both `@` empty" holds at the restart. A fact
  known only after the Land is not written: the note names what the next session checks, `main`
  at the closing, the bookmarks gone, the installed version's commit, and machine-local evidence,
  a `cmp` or the Land's output, lives in the agent-repo, published by the user's `squash-push -s
  a` after `/exit`. Provisional, on trial from **feat: vc-x1 land**.

##### Why: notes in the closing

Notes written after the Land have no clean home: a commit after it puts a non-cycle commit on the
trunk after the hard stop, and a squash into the closing rewrites the landmark just landed and
verified. The cost, notes written before the Land they describe, suits a close-out.

#### The exit-status rule is one form, and hooks guard it

- Working practices' Exit status becomes one form, the command under test bare and last, `set -o
  pipefail` first when piped, and the Rules index lists it and One command per invocation.
- The set carries its Claude Code hooks, `agent-data/bash-guard.sh`, `bash-allow.sh`, and
  `inhibit-sleep.sh`, with `agent-data/hooks.sh check|install|test`. Acquaint gains a step 2,
  Hooks, the check, the install the user's.
- `bash-allow.sh` names this family's commands and `inhibit-sleep.sh` needs systemd, so an adopter
  may carry other hooks, and `hooks.sh`'s lists are its own. From **feat: a hook enforces the
  shell rules**.

##### Why: hooks guard the rule

The rule was broken through a whole session with nothing failing, and a deny at the moment of the
slip is the one fix that does not rely on remembering it.

#### Not in it

Each run on its own:

- The record's home, `zDOING.md` in place of `TODO.md > ## In Progress`: **The cycle-record moves
  out of TODO.md into zDOING.md**.
- A rung inserted before pushed rungs: a `jj.md` recipe, once **lookup is tested on a reordered
  ladder** has its results.

Agreed. Your paste also answers the open question: `jj op log` matches up with our ids easily. Its operation ids are the same 12 hex digits our `--ops` rows show, and its `vc-x1-run:` line starts with the same 12 hex digits as our RUN column (`01a18813bf0b…`).

**Why `jj op log -n 3` reads better**
- **What `-n` counts.** jj counts operations, so `-n 3` prints 3 entries. Ours counts runs, so `-n 3` printed 2 rows, because only 2 recorded runs exist. With `--ops` it printed about 30 lines and skipped another 1,335.
- **One order.** jj is newest first all the way down. Ours lists runs newest first but a run's operations oldest first, so `01a1859dd8a2` reads 20:04:38 → 20:04:41 while the stretch below it runs 20:04:02 → 16:06.
- **Every entry describes itself.** jj prints the run's attributes on the operation that carries them, so nothing has to be grouped or explained. Our table needs KIND, the `no run` rows, and the `... N more` lines to explain itself.
- **The untagged history swamps ours.** The stable `vc-x1` records no runs, so almost everything is a `no run` stretch, and the 1,340-operation one dwarfs the two real runs. That fades once this cycle lands, but it's what you see today.

**My recommendation**

Drop `op --list` and let `jj op log` be the detailed view, as you suggested ("maybe, we remove it if it's not useful"). `undo --list` stays ours, one row per run, since only vc-x1 knows what a run is and what undo can take back. Its rows show the run id, and anyone who wants the detail runs `jj op log` and finds that id.

The rung would then keep:
- the run record's command line without the body
- `src/jj/op_history.rs`, the reader that `undo --list` needs
- the walk and the grouping by run, moved to where `undo --list` will use them

It would drop the `op` subcommand, its table, and most of `tests/cli_op_log.rs`. The rung's title and subsection would change to match, perhaps **feat: the op log is read by run**.

One catch: the open proposal **vc-x1 is the interface, jj the engine** hasn't decided whether read-only `jj op log` stays allowed. Leaning on it here makes that case: it's read-only, it's for detail, and its output is already better than ours.

This changes the agreed plan, so I'm stopping here. Should I cut `op --list` from the rung as described, or do you want something else?

Ours shows two because only two vc-x1 runs have ever been recorded in the work-repo's history, and `-n` counts runs, not operations. I counted the run ids in the work-repo's whole `jj op log`:

```
4 vc-x1-run: 01a1859dd8a2…   the commit -s b, its 4 operations
1 vc-x1-run: 01a18813bf0b…   the install, its 1 snapshot
```

Recording started with the rung that is now `@-`, and only `vc-x1-dev` records. The stable `vc-x1` (0.85.15) records nothing, and neither do raw `jj` commands. So `-n 3` asked for three runs, the walk reached the start of the history after finding two, and nothing on screen says so.

`jj op log -n 3` printed three operations: `9ff43c96db8a`, `a203de51309b` and `2a98496a9333`. It counts every operation, so the two untagged snapshots from last night fill its count. Our table hides them because they belong to no run.

Without `--ops`, a short count looks like a bug. That's the footer I proposed earlier and you haven't answered yet. For this case it would read something like:

```
2 runs, all there are; 1,355 operations recorded no run (--ops shows them)
```

Or `op --list` could go the other way and fill its count: when fewer runs exist than `-n` asks for, it shows the untagged stretches as rows, as `--ops` does now but without listing their operations.

Which do you want: the footer, stretch rows when the runs fall short, or both?

The plain version: we found only two runs because only two exist. Every earlier operation came from the stable `vc-x1` or raw `jj`, which don't record runs. The table should say so instead of leaving it silent.

I've traced the duplicate operation to its code. Here's what the 20 operations show.

**The 20 operations, newest first**
1. **`9ff43c96db8a`**: the `vc-x1-dev install` run's snapshot, tagged with its run id. This is the one tagged operation outside the commit run.
2. **15 untagged snapshots from last night**: earlier I called these raw jj commands, and that was wrong. Raw jj stamps every operation `wink@3900x`, and these carry no user. In the whole log, 543 operations are stamped `wink@3900x` and 817 carry no user, which means a vc-x1 made them through jj-lib. These came from a vc-x1 that doesn't record runs, most likely the stable 0.85.15, used while the rung was being edited. Each one snapshotted because files had changed.
3. **The last 4, the `commit -s b` run**: all share one run id and one `vc-x1-args`:
   - `2a0c7259f1f8` commit
   - `8b4e6e507d81` point bookmark → `c594f1c0`
   - `ab15ca659779` point bookmark → `c594f1c0` again, identical text, 3 seconds later
   - `76236e91c9c1` push bookmark

**What I read from them**
- **The near-twins are a wasted operation.** The second "point bookmark" moves the bookmark to where it already is, just before the push. `Session::bookmark_set` (`src/jj/session.rs:995`) commits a transaction even when nothing changes, and both the commit step and the push step call it. That's a small bug to file: it adds a step to the op log and to every future undo.
- **The body repeats on every operation.** That's the earlier build's recording, and this rung's "leave out `--body`" fixes it. Operations are never rewritten, though, so `jj op log` will show these four bodies forever. `op --list` re-renders old records by today's rules, so it shows the run as one row with its title.
- **The stamps are uneven.** vc-x1 never sets a user or host. Its transactions record the workspace (`default@`) but its snapshots don't: 427 operations versus 389. Setting the user and host through jj-lib would make our operations look like jj's own in `jj op log`. That's worth a Todo too.

**What it means for `op --list`**

`jj op log -n 20` spent 15 of its 20 entries on snapshots and showed one run's body four times. `op --list` shows the same history as two rows. So for seeing "what ran", `op --list` earns its place. It's `--ops` that duplicates `jj op log`, and does it worse. That fits what you said: keep `op --list` and drop or rethink `--ops`. The short count still wants the footer from my last message.

Three things to decide:
1. Should I drop `--ops` from this rung?
2. Do you want the footer, or untagged-stretch rows when there are fewer runs than `-n` asked for?
3. Should I file both findings as Todos: the no-op bookmark operation, and vc-x1 not stamping user, host and workspace?

The plain version: 15 of the 20 are snapshots from the stable vc-x1, not raw jj. The two near-identical entries are a real bug, a bookmark move that changes nothing. Our one-row-per-run view is clearer than `jj op log` for seeing what ran, so `op --list` looks worth keeping and `--ops` doesn't.

Your clone shows that the op log doesn't travel. Commits and change ids do.

**What came across**
- **Commits, bookmarks and descriptions:** they live in git. The clone even fetched `c594f1c0`, the rung on the cycle bookmark, not just `main`.
- **Change ids:** I checked `c594f1c0`, `c1e9e653` and `de2e9af7`, and each has the same change id in both repos (`olrmtnsw`, `qzmuxlkl`, `msxqqltw`). jj stores the change id in the git commit, so the `ochid:` trailers still resolve in a fresh clone. That's what `lookup` and the pairing rely on.

**What didn't**
- **The op log:** none of the original's ~1,360 operations made it. The clone's history starts at the clone: the empty root, then four operations. The op log lives in `.jj` and is never pushed. Your clone confirms the **undo across clones** point from the continuation notes: another clone can't see, list, or undo a run made here.

**What the clone's four operations show**
1. `add workspace 'default'`: untagged, and stamped with no user or workspace. jj-lib's workspace setup makes this operation before vc-x1 opens its own transaction. The run record covers four places that start transactions, and workspace init is a fifth it misses. Small, but it means the clone run's first operation isn't recorded as part of it.
2. `add git remote origin`, `fetch from git remote into empty repo`, and `new empty commit`: all tagged with one run id, `01a18848…`, which is the clone run. That's the recording working on a command that wasn't tested for it.

**What it means for undo**

In a fresh clone, the only run `undo --list` can offer is the clone itself. Undoing it would restore the repo to before the remote was added, which leaves an empty repo with nothing fetched. We think undo should refuse `clone` and `init` runs, since there's no "before" worth returning to; deleting the directory is the undo. Neither rule is in the plan yet.

1. Recording misses workspace init: the clone's first operation goes untagged.
2. Undo refuses `clone` and `init` runs.
3. `bookmark_set` commits an operation even when the bookmark doesn't move (last message).
4. vc-x1 doesn't stamp user, host, or workspace on its operations, and its snapshots lack even the workspace (last message).
5. Undo across clones, offered yesterday. The clone confirms it, and change ids surviving supports the `vc-x1-run:` trailer idea.

is the entry's anchor, so a citation is a link, `[title](TODO.md#<slug>)`, that the anchor check
verifies ([Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) for the text). Entries carry no number: a rank number
renumbers on every move and every citation that holds one goes stale, which is why the numbered
form was retired (2026-08-27). An entry's sub-entries, when it groups several, are bullets with a
bold title, cited by the bold text.

Example shape:

```
## Todo

### Add new feature X

The feature, in a sentence or two ([details](features.md#feature-x)).

### Fix bug Y

What is wrong and where [[1]].

7:## Prose form
8-
9-([why](rationale.md#prose-form))
10-
11-Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why* or
12-the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
13-[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
14-numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One fact
15-per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they
16-hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their
17-relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See [Semicolons](#semicolons) and [Typeable
18-punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
19-
20-Surfaces that use this shape:
21-
22-- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See [Doc
23-  comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
24-- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and agent-repo). The title is the commit-specific add-on.
25-  See [The per-rung flow](../AGENTS.md#the-per-rung-flow).
26-- The cycle-record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`. See [The In Progress
27-  block](notes.md#the-in-progress-block).
28-- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are
29-  still fine.
30-
31-Bullet *content* differs by surface:
32-
33-- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, arranged by
34-  [Commit-body form](#commit-body-form) below. What is specific to a commit:
35-  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader meets
36-    first and it answers the problem
37-  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them is
38-    a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
39-  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A bullet
40-    wanting a paragraph belongs in the cycle-record instead
41-  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
42-    live in the cycle-record, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names, each
43-    reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs here
44-- **Cycle-record / todo**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what landed
45-  and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit list. The diff
46-  is the mechanical record, the commit body the problem and solution, the cycle-record the design
47-  thinking, and none restates another.

typos. The flag's word and the config key's are the same.
  - `[cycle] closing-shape`, `"trapezoid"` or `"linear"`, is the project's default, a preference
    that belongs in the committed `.vc-config.md` with `[validate]` and `[build]`, since adopters
    choose differently. Absent, it is trapezoid, so an adopter who sets nothing sees no change.
  - The flag, then the key, then trapezoid, and `commit` prints which decided. Close-out step 5
    still has the user choose, the key only making the usual answer the default, and a stated
    preference is not the assumption about the current branch that `--closing <REV>` removed.
  - Either converts to the other while the closing is a draft, before Land, by re-parenting the
    same closing, which keeps its change id and trailer, and with the trunk unmoved its tree too,
    `REV` being in the ladder's ancestry. After Land a conversion would rewrite the trunk, so it is
    refused.
  - A linear closing cannot join a trunk that moved: the ladder would need a rebase, a rewrite of
    published commits into a tree no validation saw. `--land` already refuses a moved trunk, so
    the refusal is the whole answer, and the way out is the reshape rung's command, then a
    validation, then the closing. A rebase inside a linear closing would be the hidden multi-step
    operation the cycle removes.
  - The v0.3.1 proposal said keep separate goes, and its section **The closing is a trapezoid or
    linear, and converts** now keeps it as the linear shape and names the flag and the key, edited
    at the closing rung's review when this rung was added, so the proposal leads the flag by one
    rung.
  - Its own rung after the closing's shapes, since `--land` lands both.
- `vc-x1 reparent`, wink's call at the closing rung's review (2026-10-23): parent fix-ups get their
  own command, since `merge` is the wrong verb for removing one.
  - `--target <REV>`, any committed node, with `--add`, `--remove`, or `--set`, one jj-lib rebase
    of it onto its new parent list, its descendants rebased, the list printed before and after,
    and a failure restored from a snapshot. `merge`'s guards carry over: no cycle, no parent at or
    below the target, `--ignore-immutable` for a jj-immutable one.
  - `--remove` changes the tree: the target keeps its own diff, and what the removed parent brought
    is gone from it, so it prints what was dropped. The last parent is never removed, `--set`
    being the way to replace it, and a conflicted result is reported and left.
  - `merge` stays as the short form of `--add`, its tests and `commit --closing`'s use of its
    primitive unchanged, and may retire into `reparent` later.
- The closing's undo, the Todo's lean, for a closing made without `--land`, a flag
  or a sibling command settled at its rung. A Land's undo, after its push, waits for a real mistake.

### A bookmark set to where it is commits no operation

(agent, 2026-10-29) `Session::bookmark_set` commits a transaction whether or not the bookmark moves,
so a `commit -s b` leaves two identical "point bookmark ... to commit ..." operations, the commit's
advance and push's, 3 s apart. Found in `jj op log` at the rung **feat: op lists each run and its
operations** of **feat: undo takes back the last vc-x1 run**.

- A transaction with no change is dropped rather than committed, `repo_mut().has_changes()`, in
  `bookmark_set` or in `finish_tx` for every caller.
- Each wasted operation is one more line in the op log and one more step an undo walks back.

### The run record misses workspace init

(agent, 2026-10-29) A `clone` run's first operation in each repo, jj-lib's `add workspace
'default'`, carries no run record, since it is made before vc-x1 opens a transaction. The record is
set at four places, `Session::start_tx` and the snapshot and the two git imports, and workspace
init is a fifth. Seen in a fresh `vc-x1-dev clone`, whose other three operations per repo carry
the run.

- Tag it, or treat the operation before a run's first as the run's base, which is what an undo
  restores to either way.
- `init` makes the same operation and is the other case to check.

### vc-x1 stamps no user, host, or workspace on its operations

(agent, 2026-10-29) In `jj op log` raw jj's operations read `wink@3900x default@` and vc-x1's read
`@`, with no user or host, and its snapshots carry no workspace either. In this work-repo 543
operations are raw jj's, 427 vc-x1's with a workspace, and 389 vc-x1's without.

- Set the user and host through jj-lib's settings, as jj-cli does, so vc-x1's operations read as
  jj's own, the run record saying which run made them.
- The snapshot path sets the workspace as the transactions do.
- A missing stamp tells vc-x1's operations from raw jj's today, and is how a stable vc-x1's
  untagged ones were recognized. The run record replaces that test.

### undo refuses clone and init runs

(wink + agent, 2026-10-29) In a fresh clone the one run `undo --list` offers is the clone, and
undoing it would restore each repo to its first operation, no remote and nothing fetched. There is
no state before a `clone` or an `init` worth returning to, and removing the directory is its undo.

- `undo` refuses a run whose command is `clone` or `init`, naming why, and `undo --list` marks it
  or leaves it out.
- For **feat: undo takes back the last vc-x1 run** or a cycle after it.

### undo across clones

(wink + agent, 2026-10-28, confirmed 2026-10-29) The op log is local to `.jj` and never pushed, so a
run made in one clone cannot be listed or undone from another. A fresh `vc-x1-dev clone` of this
pair begins both op logs at the clone, none of the original's operations carried. Commits carry
their change ids, `c594f1c0`, `c1e9e653`, and `de2e9af7` identical in both, so `ochid:` trailers
resolve in a clone.

- The idea: a `vc-x1-run: <id>` trailer on the commits a run makes, so a clone finds a run's
  commits by their trailer where it has no op log to read.
- What a clone could undo is open: the commits and pushes a trailer finds, not the local operations
  only the original saw.

### Dry runs interleave: commit, push, and sync

message.content: The last two, "undo refuses .." & "undo across clones" should be in this cycle, don't you agree?

content.text:
I agree on the first and would keep the second as a Todo.

**"undo refuses clone and init runs": yes, it belongs in this cycle.** It's a rule about which runs undo will take, so it fits the rung **feat: undo restores the repos to before the last run**: one check on the run's command, one test, and a line in `undo --list`. Leaving it out would ship an undo that can empty a fresh clone.

**"undo across clones": I'd keep it out.** This cycle's undo works by restoring each repo's op log to before the run, and another clone has no op log to restore. Undoing across clones needs a different mechanism:
- A `vc-x1-run:` trailer on every commit a run makes. That changes `commit` and `push`, and touches the agent-files' trailer rules.
- An undo that reverts commits and rolls back pushes found through that trailer, rather than restoring operations. It's a second undo with its own design questions: what counts as the run's commits after a rebase, and what happens when someone has built on them.

Adding that would roughly double the cycle. What I'd add here instead is the boundary: `undo --list` and the undo docs say that undo sees only runs made in this clone. That small part fits the planned rung **docs: undo is how a mistake is taken back**.

If you agree, I'll:
1. Move "undo refuses clone and init runs" into the cycle record: the rule goes in the Solution, the check in the Acceptance check, and the test in the restore rung's subsection. Then I'll delete its Todo.
2. Keep "undo across clones" as a Todo, add a line saying this cycle states the boundary, and note the boundary in the docs rung's plan.

If you'd rather have cross-clone undo in this cycle anyway, it would come as one or more new rungs after **feat: undo rolls back the last run's pushes**, and I'd want to settle the trailer design with you first.

The plain version: refusing to undo a clone or init is a small rule that fits this cycle. Undo from another clone needs a whole second mechanism, because a clone has no op log to restore. I'd keep that as a Todo and only make undo say plainly that it can't see other clones' runs.

message.content: On "undo across clones": I don't understand this "The idea: a `vc-x1-run: <id>` trailer on the commits a run makes, .."

content.text:
I wrote that line too tersely. Here's the idea at more length.

**The problem it addresses**

The run id lives only in the op log, as an attribute on each jj operation. The op log stays in `.jj` on this machine. So when you push and someone clones, the commits travel, but nothing on them says which run made them. Your fresh clone showed this: it has `c594f1c0`, but nothing in it links that commit to run `01a1859dd8a2`.

**What a trailer is**

A trailer is a `key: value` line at the end of a commit message, like the `ochid:` line vc-x1 already stamps to name a commit's partner in the other repo. The idea is that vc-x1 also stamps the run id on every commit a run makes. The last rung's work-repo commit would then end:

```
feat: each vc-x1 write records its run in the op log

A vc-x1 run leaves operations ...

Solution: ... See details in zDOING.md.

ochid: /.agent-session/<agent change id>
vc-x1-run: 01a1859dd8a27bcfbeff811552dbdd6f
```

Its agent-repo partner would carry the same `vc-x1-run:` line. The id would be in the commits themselves, so it would survive push and clone, and any clone could find a run's commits with `git log --grep 'vc-x1-run: 01a1859dd8a2'`.

**Why it doesn't get you far**
- **Only commits carry it.** A run that just moves or pushes a bookmark, deletes one, or squashes into an existing commit makes no new commit, so it leaves nothing to find. Most of what undo needs to reverse (bookmark positions, what was pushed) isn't in commits at all.
- **Finding isn't undoing.** In the other clone, undo couldn't restore operations, since that clone never had them. It could only revert the commits or move bookmarks back, which is a different and riskier operation.
- **It adds noise for everyone.** Every commit message would grow a line that matters only to undo.

So the trailer would answer "which commits did this run make?" from any clone. That's useful for `lookup` or auditing, but it falls well short of undo across clones. On reflection, the Todo overstates it. I'd rewrite the entry as: "undo works only in the clone where the run happened, and the op log can't travel. A `vc-x1-run:` trailer would let any clone find the commits a run made, but it wouldn't make those runs undoable there." Or drop the trailer idea from it entirely.

Which would you like: rewrite it that way, drop the trailer idea, or drop the Todo?

The plain version: the idea was to write the run's id into each commit message so it travels with the commits. That would let another clone see which commits a run made, but not undo the run, because undo also needs the local history that never leaves this machine.

content.text:
No. The run id is vc-x1's own and has nothing to do with jj or with the vc-x1 binary's commit. What it is:

**Where it comes from**

Each time you invoke vc-x1, it makes a new id at startup (`RunId::now()` in `src/jj/run.rs`). It's 128 bits:
- **The first 48 bits are the start time**, in Unix milliseconds. That's why the ids look alike and sort by time. Decoding the commit run's `01a1859dd8a2` gives 2026-10-29 03:04:36 UTC, which is 20:04:36 your time, two seconds before its first operation in the op log.
- **The other 80 bits are mostly random**, so two runs in the same millisecond still differ. This is the UUID v7 layout.

**What it means**

It names one invocation of vc-x1, say `vc-x1 commit -s b --title ...`, from start to exit. That's all.

**Why we need it**

jj has no notion of a run. It knows operations: each one has an id (`9ff43c96db8a`, `2a0c7259f1f8`, ...) and is one atomic change to one repo. One vc-x1 invocation makes several. Your `commit -s b` made four in the work-repo (commit, point bookmark twice, push) plus more in the agent-repo. The run id is what ties them together. vc-x1 stamps it on every operation it makes, in every repo, as the `vc-x1-run:` attribute you saw in `jj op log`. That lets undo say "take back run `01a1859dd8a2`" and find every operation in both repos that belongs to it.

So the link already exists: run id → jj operations, through the op log. The binary that did the run isn't recorded. The record holds the run id, the command, the command line, and a format number, but not vc-x1's version or commit. We could add that if you want it.

**What the trailer idea was**

It would link the run id to the commits the run created in your repos (`c594f1c0` and its agent partner), not to vc-x1's own commit. Today that link exists only through the op log, which stays on this machine. A trailer would put it in the commit message, where it travels. As I said last time, that tells another clone which commits a run made, but it doesn't make the run undoable there.

The plain version: the run id is a timestamp-plus-random number that vc-x1 makes each time it runs and stamps on every jj operation that run makes, so undo can find all the pieces of one command. It doesn't involve jj's ids or vc-x1's own commit.

message.content: So I think what you're saying is that the run id is one invocation of a particular vc-x1 sub-command and parameters. So if we want to undo a particular `vc-x1-dev commit -sb --title .. ` it's not 1 jj op it's a series of them and we can identify the exact series by matching the run <id> and reverse that set and we're done.

content.text:
Yes, with three refinements before "we're done".

**What you have right**

One invocation of a subcommand with its parameters is one run. It makes a series of jj operations, possibly in both repos, and every one carries the same run id. Matching the id finds exactly that series and nothing else.

**The refinements**
1. **Undo restores to before the run rather than reversing each operation.** For the last run it's simpler and safer to put each repo back to the operation just before the run's first one, which is `jj op restore` done through jj-lib, in every repo the run touched. That gives the same result as reversing the series, in one step per repo. It's the rung **feat: undo restores the repos to before the last run**.
2. **Pushes don't come back with the restore.** The op log is local. Restoring it moves your local bookmarks back, but the remote still has what the run pushed. Your `commit -s b` ended with "push bookmark ... to git remote origin", so undoing it also means pushing the bookmark back to where it was, with a lease so nobody else's work is overwritten. That's the rung **feat: undo rolls back the last run's pushes**.
3. **"The last run" is the easy case.** If other runs came after the one you want to undo, restoring to before it would also throw away theirs. Undoing an earlier run means reverting just its changes, and only when the later work doesn't depend on them. That's the rung **feat: undo takes back a chosen run when what followed is independent**.

One more care point: the restore mustn't overwrite the files on disk. Edits made since the run, like your uncommitted work, stay in the working copy.

So for undoing your last `vc-x1-dev commit -s b --title ...`:
1. Find its operations by run id in both repos.
2. Restore each repo to the operation just before its first one.
3. Push each moved bookmark back to where it was before the run: the work-repo bookmark and the agent-repo `main`.

That's the whole job, and it's what the remaining rungs build in that order.

The plain version: yes, the run id picks out exactly the jj operations one command made. Undo then rewinds each repo to just before them, and also pushes back anything the command published, since rewinding is local and doesn't touch the remote.

content.text:
I agree, and I think your rule is better than the one we agreed yesterday, "undo every repo the run touched or none". Both of your worries are real.

**Concurrency is a real risk.** The agent-repo is written all the time, because Claude Code appends to the session transcript while I work, and I'd be the one running the undo. A restore rewinds the agent-repo's state while that file is still growing. jj copes with concurrent operations by merging them, but if the restore wrote the old file contents to disk, it could cut off the transcript in the middle of the session. We planned to leave files on disk alone, but that is the riskiest thing to rely on in the one repo that is always being written.

**Missing pieces are a real loss.** Even with the files kept, undoing the agent half removes its commit and pushes the agent `main` back. The remote, and every clone after it, then lose that part of the conversation, while the conversation itself goes on as if it happened. The agent-repo is a record, and a record shouldn't lose entries.

**Never undo the agent-repo**

Undo would touch the work-repo only. It would make the plan simpler:
- **No concurrency problem.** Undo never writes the repo that is being written.
- **The push rollback covers only the work bookmark.** The agent `main` is never pushed backwards.
- **Agent-only runs (`commit -s a`, `squash-push -s a`) aren't undoable.** The agent-repo is fixed by moving forward, like the messages repo's append-only rule. `squash-push -s a` still folds into the agent tip, but that adds transcript and loses nothing.

**What it costs**

This was why I proposed undoing both repos. After undoing a `commit -s b`, the agent commit stays, and its `ochid:` trailer names a work change that's gone. Today `lookup` treats a dangling trailer as an error (`dr1_dangling_trailer_is_an_error`), and validation may too. So the plan needs:
- **lookup and validation accept a trailer that names a change undo took back.** They warn rather than fail, in line with "warn rather than refuse". jj still holds the hidden change locally, so it can tell "taken back" from "never existed".
- **The undo states it in the agent-repo.** The undo run's own output says which agent commit now names a taken-back change. The session goes on and its next agent commit carries that, so the record explains the dangling trailer instead of hiding it.

**Plan changes if you agree**
1. In the Solution: undo acts on the work-repo alone. The agent-repo is never undone, and you get the reason, concurrency and the record. Yesterday's both-or-none rule is replaced, with the reason it lost.
2. Undo's `-s`: it either goes away or accepts `w` only. I lean towards dropping it, so there's nothing to choose wrong.
3. The push-rollback rung covers the work bookmark only.
4. A new or widened rung lets lookup and validation accept a trailer naming a taken-back change.
5. **undo refuses clone and init runs** moves into the cycle as discussed. It now applies to the work side only.

Shall I write these into the cycle record?

The plain version: undoing the agent-repo risks clobbering the conversation while it's being written, and it erases part of the record. So undo only ever rewinds the work-repo. The cost is that an agent commit can point at a work commit that was undone, so lookup and validation must accept that and say so rather than fail.

message.content: And yes, we now have dangling ochid's on the agent-repo pointing to non-existent work-repo commits. A possible solution is we never revert either repo we simply "fork" off an older commit leaving dangling commits on the work-repo, probably with a permanent "dangling-<id>" where the id is the order id like vc-x1-run uses. Thoughts only.

content.text:
I like it. It turns undo into a forward move instead of a rewind, and that removes most of what has been worrying us. Here's my read.

**What it fixes**
- **No trailer dangles.** The run's commits stay, reachable by the permanent bookmark and pushed, so every `ochid:` resolves in this clone and in any other. `lookup` and validation need no changes, and `dr1_dangling_trailer_is_an_error` stays right.
- **Neither repo is reverted, and neither is the op log.** Undo becomes a normal run: move the work bookmark back, put the permanent bookmark where it was, and push both. No `op restore`, so there's no concurrency question in either repo, and the agent-repo stays linear.
- **Nothing is lost, and undo can be undone.** Moving the bookmark back to the kept tip is a redo, done the same way.
- **It matches a rule we already have.** v0.3.1's "dead ends land" keeps every rung reachable for the same reason: agent commits name work commits, so dropping them leaves trailers naming nothing. This applies that rule to a single run.
- **It's simpler to build.** It needs only bookmark moves and a lease-protected push, which vc-x1 already has. Restoring the op log without clobbering files on disk was the hardest part of the plan.

**What it raises**
- **The name.** Once something has a bookmark it's no longer dangling, and in git "dangling" means unreachable, which is the opposite. I'd suggest `undone/<run-id>`, using the id of the run that was taken back. That says what it is, links to the op log locally, and sorts by time as you wanted. The slash groups them so `jj bookmark list` and GitHub can filter them. A git tag fits "permanent" even better, since tags don't move. We think jj-lib can write one through its git backend, but that needs checking.
- **Clutter.** One ref per undo, forever, on the remote. Undos should be rare, so we think that's fine, and a retention rule can come later if it isn't.
- **The working copy.** Undoing `commit` puts its changes back into `@` as uncommitted edits, so `@` holds the same content as the kept commit. Committing again makes a second, separate commit, and the kept one records the first attempt. That's honest, but it should be stated.
- **Runs that rewrite rather than add** (`squash`, a re-describe through `commit -r`). The pre-run version is hidden in jj, not on any line. Undo would bring it back as the bookmark's target and keep the rewritten one under `undone/<id>`. Same mechanism, but those runs need their own tests.
- **Runs that make no commits** (a push, a bookmark move). There's nothing to keep, so undo just moves the bookmark back and no `undone/` ref is made.
- **The trunk.** Cycles run on bookmarks, so forks hang off the cycle line, and at Land `main` stays clean. In gitk the graph shows each undo as a short side branch, which we think is a feature.
- **An earlier run with later runs after it** (rung p5) stays hard. Forking would mean replaying the later commits onto the older base, which rewrites published commits. The fork idea makes undoing the last run clean, but it doesn't make that case easy.

**What changes in the plan**

The rung "restores the repos to before the last run" becomes "forks the line back to before the last run". The push-rollback rung stays, and now also pushes the `undone/` ref. Undo acts on the work-repo only. The both-or-none rule and the trailer-tolerance work both go away. `undo --list` and the op-log reader stay, since undo still has to find a run's operations to know which bookmarks it moved and where they were before.

The plain version: instead of erasing what a run did, undo moves the bookmark back and pins the abandoned commits under a permanent name like `undone/<run-id>`. Nothing disappears, the agent-repo's links keep working, neither repo is rewound, and the costs are a growing list of `undone/` refs and some care with commands that rewrite commits.

message.content:
Should this be done on development and release branches? On release branches the general rule should be you never
delete anything. Instead you do a new release in a manner that resolves the issue as expeditiously as possible.
Then you might "hide" the bad release or change it's name such as bad-release-vX.Y.Z.

On development branches do what you like, if you don't care about dangling references between agent and work then
delete the work commits using undo/revert. If you do then don't and create a undone/<id>.

content.text:
Yes. That split matches a line the rules already draw, and it settles where each kind of undo belongs.

**The line is already there.** The agent-files say a cycle is a draft on its bookmark until Land, and after Land its commits are permanent. So your two kinds map onto what exists:
- **Development branches** are the cycle bookmarks, and drafts. Undo is allowed there.
- **The release branch** is the trunk, `main` or `[cycle] trunk`, holding everything landed. Undo refuses anything that moved it or rewrote a commit on it. The fix is a new cycle. The tool can tell the two apart by checking whether a commit is already on `main@origin`, so there's no list of branch names to maintain.
- **The agent-repo is release-like all the time.** Its `main` only moves forward, which is why never undoing it felt right. It follows your release rule, not the development one.

**Release branches**
- **Fix forward:** a new cycle and a new version, as quickly as the fix allows. That fits the protocol as it stands, since a cycle can be small.
- **Mark the bad release, don't rename it.** A rename is a delete and a create, and every clone that already fetched the old name keeps it, so the rename doesn't reach the people it's meant to warn. Adding a marker beside it does reach them, say a `bad-release/vX.Y.Z` ref or a note in the next release saying what was wrong. It's the same idea as `cargo yank`: the release stays for anyone who depends on it, flagged so nobody new picks it up. Whether vc-x1 tags releases at all today I'd have to check. The version lives in `Cargo.toml` and a release is a Land plus an install.
- **This changes an old note.** The cycle's deliberation said "a Land's undo, after its push, waits for a real mistake". Under this rule a Land isn't undoable at all: undo refuses it and names the fix-forward path.

**Development branches**
- **Keep or discard per undo.** Discard removes the run's commits. Keep moves the bookmark back and pins them under `undone/<run-id>`.
- **We think the default should come from the references, not a fixed setting:**
  - nothing points at the run's commits (a work-only commit that was never pushed, with no agent trailer naming it): discard, which is harmless
  - an agent trailer names them, as after any `commit -s b`: keep by default, and discard only on request, with a warning that names the trailer it leaves dangling ("warn rather than refuse")
- A flag could override either way, perhaps `--keep` and `--discard`, plus a config key for a project that never cares about the references.

**How the cycle changes**
- The undo rungs act on cycle lines only, and refuse runs that touched the trunk or an already-landed commit.
- The restore rung gains both outcomes, keep (`undone/<id>`) and discard, with the default worked out as above.
- A docs line: release mistakes are fixed forward, with a marker on the bad release.
- The release marker itself, `bad-release/` or something like yank, is probably its own Todo rather than part of this cycle.

The plain version: on a cycle's branch, undo may delete the run's commits when nothing refers to them, and keeps them under `undone/<id>` when an agent commit does. On `main` and in the agent-repo, nothing is ever undone. A bad release gets a fixed release after it, and a marker saying the old one is bad, not a rename.

message.content:
You like to use the word land, but it's always been nebulous to me. In a large company releasing
was not a single step, it went through a formal process of testing over a period of time.
In our conversations when you say "Land" you always assume you mean "Land on main" and I sometimes
reply that way. But what it your definition of "Land".

content.text:
In this project "Land" has a fixed meaning, and it bundles three steps that a large company keeps separate. That's why it reads as vague.

**What the agent-files say**

`AGENTS.md` Terminology: "Land: the sequence that makes a cycle permanent, on the user's go at the close-out. Before it the cycle is a draft on its bookmark, after it the commits are permanent."

Concretely, in the v0.3.1 form:
1. Sync both repos.
2. `vc-x1 commit --closing <BM> --land`: fast-forward `main` to the closing commit and push it.
3. Delete the cycle's bookmark, locally and on the remote.
4. `vc-x1 install`: build the release binary and put it on this machine's PATH.

So by definition, "Land" means landing on `main`. There's no other kind, and that's why we both use it that way.

**What it bundles**

In a company these are separate stages, each with its own gate:
- **Integrate:** the change joins the trunk that everyone builds on. Our step 2.
- **Release:** a version is cut, tested over time, and approved. We have nothing separate for this. The closing commit carries the version bump, so the moment it lands on `main`, that commit *is* release `X.Y.Z`. The only testing is validation before every push, plus the optional candidate install the v0.3.1 proposal describes, tested off the PATH before `--land`.
- **Deploy:** the release is put where it runs. Our step 4, for one machine.

For one person and one machine, collapsing them works. But it's why "Land" feels like more than "merge to main": it also is the release and the deployment.

**What this means for the undo rule**

My last answer treated `main` as the release branch, which blurred two things:
- **The integration trunk (`main`):** it's shared and permanent. Even in companies, a mistake there is fixed with a new commit (a revert or a fix), never by rewriting. So "never delete" applies, but for a reason of its own: other people and clones build on it.
- **A release:** a version shipped to users, such as crates.io or an installed binary on other machines. Here your rule applies fully: fix forward with a new release, and mark the bad one. In this project, releases and `main` happen to be the same commits, but they wouldn't be in a company process with release branches cut from the trunk.

The undo rule holds either way: never undo on `main` or anything landed. But the vocabulary should be able to say which of the three you mean.

**Sharpening the term**

We could narrow "Land" to integrate alone, make "release" its own step (today a no-op, the version bump on `main`), and make "install" its own, so a later project could add a testing period between them. That's an agent-files proposal, so it would be a Todo, not part of this cycle. Shall I file it?

The plain version: "Land" here means one go-step that merges the finished cycle into `main`, pushes it, deletes the cycle's bookmark, and installs the new binary. That's integrating, releasing, and deploying all at once, which works for a solo project but explains why the word feels vague next to a company's staged release process.

content.text:
You're right, and the tool's definition is narrower and more general than the one I gave. The tool and the rules disagree, and that gap is probably what made "Land" feel vague.

**`vc-x1 land`, from its help**
- Fast-forward `--onto` to `--source` and push it.
- Delete the cycle's bookmark, locally and on `origin`, unless `--skip`.
- All the checks run before anything moves.
- `--onto` is any local bookmark at its `origin` position that `--source` descends from: "a bushy tree lands anywhere". A cycle can land onto another cycle's bookmark, not only onto `main`.
- It only fast-forwards. A merge is `commit --closing`'s job.
- The install is not part of it: "The install stays `vc-x1 install`, after."

So the tool's Land is just the integrate step, onto whatever line the cycle branched from. It doesn't release or install, and it doesn't require `main`.

**The rules' Land**

`AGENTS.md` defines it as "the sequence that makes a cycle permanent", and Close-out step 6 spells it out as sync, reshape, fast-forward `main`, install, and delete the bookmark. That bundles the install and assumes `main`. That's the definition I gave you, and it's older than the tool's.

**Why it matters for undo**

"Landed" doesn't mean "permanent". If cycle B lands onto cycle A's bookmark, B's commits are only as permanent as A, which is still a draft until A lands on the trunk. So the undo rule shouldn't ask "was this landed?". It should ask "is this commit on the trunk's remote, `main@origin`?". The check I proposed already works that way, but my wording, "never undo anything landed", was wrong. It should be "never undo anything on the trunk".

**What I'd change in the wording**
- **Land:** the tool's meaning. Integrate a finished cycle into the line named by `--onto` (fast-forward, push, delete the bookmark), usually `main`, but any line it branched from.
- **Permanent:** on the trunk's remote, not "landed".
- **Install:** its own close-out step after Land, as the tool already treats it.
- **Release:** today it's the version bump on the trunk, and has no separate step until a project needs one.

That's an agent-files proposal: Terminology, Close-out step 6, and the v0.3.1 Land text. I'd file it as a Todo, or fold it into the v0.3.1 proposal, which already rewrites Land. Folding is probably better, since v0.3.1 is the form we're running now. Which do you prefer?

content.text:
Yes. `@-` with an empty `@` is simpler, and it's what the rest of vc-x1 already assumes. `push` moves the line's bookmark to `@-`, and `commit --closing` usually names `@-`.

**Why it's better**
- **Local, not global.** Today's default, "the one local bookmark besides `--onto`", depends on every bookmark in the repo and fails once there are two. `@-` is what you're sitting on.
- **An empty `@` means you land exactly what was validated.** Validation runs on the working copy. If `@` is empty, the working copy's tree is `@-`'s tree, so the commit that lands is the one validated. A non-empty `@` means there's work that won't go along, or a tree no validation saw.
- **It fits the usual flow.** `commit --closing` without `--land` leaves the closing at `@-` with an empty `@` on top, so a bare `land --onto main -s b` lands it.

**Details to settle**
- **The empty-`@` check applies to the work-repo only.** The agent `@` is never empty because the session is always writing to it, and `-s b` publishes the agent `main` as it stands.
- **The check applies only to the default.** An explicit `--source` says what to land, so `@` doesn't matter. The refusal would name `--source` as the way past it.
- **The bookmark to delete is found as today**, from `@-` now: its bookmark, else its nearest parent's above `--onto`, with several refused and listed.
- **A merge `@` (two parents) is refused**, since `@-` is ambiguous there.
- **Refuse rather than warn** for a non-empty `@`. A land is pushed and permanent on the trunk, so it's not one of the "warn, the user can review before the push" cases.

The help would become:

```
--source <BM|REV>
    The cycle's last commit, a bookmark or a revision [default: @-, with @ empty]
```

This is new work that arrived mid-cycle, so you pick where it goes: a `## Todo` entry for its own small cycle, or a rung inserted into this one. It isn't about undo, so I'd make it a Todo. It may also belong with the Land wording fix in the v0.3.1 proposal, since both change what Land means in practice. Which do you want?

The plain version: yes. `land` without `--source` should land the commit you're on, `@-`, and refuse if you have uncommitted changes, so what lands is exactly what you validated. I'd file it as its own small Todo rather than add it to the undo cycle.

content.text:
I think "there is no undo" is the right principle. It's what the other rules have been reaching for: dead-end cycles land, the messages repo is append-only, and a closed cycle record is never amended. Here's how I'd think it through.

**The principle**

The rule isn't really "never rewrite". It's "never drop content the agent made or a trailer names". Squashing or folding keeps the content and is fine. Restoring the op log to before a run drops content and isn't. Your split then falls out:
- **Touched by the agent, or named by a trailer:** never deleted, only abandoned forward.
- **Human-only, referenced by nothing:** do anything. jj already handles this with `jj undo` and `jj op restore`, so vc-x1 doesn't need its own undo for it. Telling "the agent was active" apart mechanically is hard, but "a trailer names it" is easy to check. We think the reference check is the test the tool can actually make, with "agent active" left to the person.

**Abandoning with `dead-end-<id>`**

This is the `undone/<id>` idea under a name that fits existing vocabulary. "Dead end" already means "kept, landed, recorded, not continued" in v0.3.1. The steps:
1. Put `dead-end-<id>` at the abandoned tip and push it, so every trailer still resolves.
2. Move the cycle's bookmark back to the chosen commit. It's a draft, so this is a lease-protected push.
3. `commit -s b` on top records the decision in both repos, so the record reads in order: what was tried, that it was dropped, what comes next.

v0.3.1's dead-end closing ends a whole cycle. This is the same act for the tail of a ladder. One name for both would be good.

**Paired bookmarks wouldn't buy an agent-side undo**

The agent-repo's content is the session transcripts, and Claude Code keeps appending to those same files on disk. If you moved the agent bookmark back to a common point, the next agent commit would contain the whole transcript again, abandoned part included, because the file never got shorter. So rewinding the agent-repo changes its commit ancestry but not its content, and the conversation reappears in the next commit. Add the concurrency risk and the lost-record risk from before, and paired bookmarks cost a lot for something that undoes itself. The agent-repo is a log, and a log only moves forward.

**Deleting in the middle**

Mechanically, jj can do it: abandon a commit and its descendants are rebased. They even keep their change ids, so the agent trailers naming later rungs would still resolve. But every descendant becomes a new tree that no validation saw, later rungs that built on the removed change conflict, and published commits get rewritten. You're right that it's not worth it. The forward version is the standard one: a **revert**, a new commit at the tip that applies the inverse of the bad change. It's simple, it keeps everything, it's reviewable, and it's how `main` gets fixed anyway. The rung "undo takes back a chosen run when what followed is independent" would really be "revert".

**What's left of this cycle**

Its title is "undo takes back the last vc-x1 run", and under this principle that undo doesn't exist. What it built still has value:
- **The run record** is pushed, and useful for auditing and for finding what a command did.
- **`op --list`** shows the history by run.
- Both would also help an `abandon` command pick the point to go back to.

The two ways I see it ending:
- **Rescope the cycle** to abandon (a dead end for a ladder's tail) and revert. The opening and the first rung keep their pushed titles, and the rename reaches only the record and the rungs not yet pushed.
- **Close it as a dead end** after this rung, keeping the run record and `op --list` and recording why undo was dropped. Abandon and revert become new Todos and their own cycle.

I lean towards the dead-end close. The cycle's premise changed, and v0.3.1 defines that outcome precisely.

The plain version: anything the agent touched is a record, so nothing gets undone. A dropped tail of a branch is parked under a permanent `dead-end-<id>` bookmark with a commit noting it, and a bad change in the middle is fixed with a revert commit. Rewinding the agent-repo is pointless anyway, because its transcript files keep everything and would just come back in the next commit.

For example, use pattern: "[MyApp]" to filter for application-specific logs rather than reading all console output.

## Alerts and dialogs

IMPORTANT: Do not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or browser modal dialogs through your actions. These browser dialogs block all further browser events and will prevent the extension from receiving any subsequent commands. Instead, when possible, use console.log for debugging and then use the mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages tool to read those log messages. If a page has dialog-triggering elements:
1. Avoid clicking buttons or links that may trigger alerts (e.g., "Delete" buttons with confirmation dialogs)
2. If you must interact with such elements, warn the user first that this may interrupt the session
3. Use mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool to check for and dismiss any existing dialogs before proceeding

If you accidentally trigger a dialog and lose responsiveness, inform the user they need to manually dismiss it in the browser.

## Avoid rabbit holes and loops

When using browser automation tools, stay focused on the specific task. If you encounter any of the following, stop and ask the user for guidance:
- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration
- Browser tool calls failing or returning errors after 2-3 attempts
- No response from the browser extension
- Page elements not responding to clicks or input
- Pages not loading or timing out
- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

Explain what you attempted, what went wrong, and ask how the user would like to proceed. Do not keep retrying the same failing browser action or explore unrelated pages without checking in first.

## Tab context and session startup

IMPORTANT: At the start of each browser automation session, call mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp first to get information about the user's current browser tabs. Use this context to understand what the user might want to work with before creating new tabs.

Never reuse tab IDs from a previous/other session. Follow these guidelines:
1. Only reuse an existing tab if the user explicitly asks to work with it
2. Otherwise, create a new tab with mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
3. If a tool returns an error indicating the tab doesn't exist or is invalid, call tabs_context_mcp to get fresh tab IDs
4. When a tab is closed by the user or a navigation error occurs, call tabs_context_mcp to see what tabs are available

Write code that reads like the surrounding code: match its comment density, naming, and idiom.

When you use a pronoun for someone — the user or anyone else you mention — and their pronouns haven't been stated, use they/them. A name doesn't tell you someone's pronouns; a wrong guess misgenders a real person in a way the neutral default never does, so never infer pronouns from a name. This applies to all user-visible text, including visible thinking.

For actions that are hard to reverse or outward-facing, confirm first unless durably authorized or explicitly told to proceed without asking; approval in one context doesn't extend to the next. Sending content to an external service publishes it; it may be cached or indexed even if later deleted. Before deleting or overwriting, look at the target. Report outcomes faithfully: if tests fail, say so with the output; if a step was skipped, say that; when something is done and verified, state it plainly without hedging.

# Session-specific guidance
