- No re-describe without coordinating: never `jj describe` a published or trailer-carrying
  commit ([Re-describing](agent-data/jj.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer)).
- Prose style: durable text is in the prose form, typeable punctuation included ([Prose
  form](agent-data/prose.md#prose-form)).
- One title per step: the ladder rung and the commit title are verbatim identical
  ([Conventional-commit shape](agent-data/prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit)).
- Alert on unwrap: say so when introducing an `unwrap` / `expect` / `unwrap_or*` site, with its
  `// OK: ...` comment ([`// OK` comments](agent-data/code.md#-ok--comments-on-unwrap-calls-rust)).

## Acquaint

What a session does first, at its start and whenever the user says "acquaint" or "reacquaint",
in this order ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#acquaint)):

1. custom.md: when there is one, read it, and do what it asks for at acquaint
   ([custom.md](#custommd)).
2. Hooks: `bash agent-data/hooks.sh check`, and what it finds missing, different, or
   unregistered is reported for the user to install ([Working practices](#working-practices)).
3. Repo check: look at each repo of the workspace for the four findings below, and report what is
   found before anything else. Nothing is opened, pushed, rebased, committed, or discarded until
   the user says how to proceed.
   - Not up to date: a repo whose `main` is behind, ahead of, or diverged from its remote's, as
     the look reports it ([Sync](#sync)), run again with `--bookmark <bookmark>` when a cycle is
     in flight. A look that fails is reported as the check not made.
   - Uncommitted work: a work-repo `@` that is not empty, as `jj st` prints it. What the
     continuation notes account for, the notes themselves or a rung in flight they describe, is
     theirs to direct at step 4, and any other change is a finding. The agent-repo's `@` holds the
     session's own data and is never one.
   - Work off `main`: commits on a bookmark, a cycle's or any other, that do not descend from the
     remote's `main`. The user is told, and a rebase onto `main` is suggested.
   - Conflicts: a conflicted commit or working copy, as `jj st` and `jj log -r 'conflicts()'` show
     them. The acquaint stops there and the user is informed.
4. TODO.md: read the acquaint slice ([File
   reads](agent-data/notes.md#file-reads-read-the-slice-you-need)), the continuation notes first,
   each acted on, filed or kept, and the section reset ([Todo
   format](agent-data/notes.md#todo-format)).
5. Report: say where things stand, the cycle in flight or the top of `## Todo`, and wait.

## Sync

One command, `vc-x1 sync --scope=both`, brings both repos up to date, each `main` at the commit
its remote's `main` is at. It runs at the moments a cycle depends on `main`, and what it prints
is reported ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#sync)):

- Acquaint looks: with `--dry-run`, which moves nothing, so each repo is reported as found.
- Opening syncs: as its first step, which is its rung's step 0, so the cycle's bookmark is
  created on an up-to-date `main`.
- Closing syncs: at its rung's step 0, so the record and version it carries are made from an
  up-to-date `main`. A rung between may sync at its step 0, the agent's or the user's call.
- Land syncs: as its first step, and a `main` the sync moved stops the Land.

A sync that fails or holds a repo back stops the step until the user says how to proceed, as does
one at a rung's step 0 that moved a `main`, and `--force` and `--rebase` are the user's to ask
for.

## Cycle protocol

How a [cycle](#terminology) runs ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#cycle-protocol)). Its record is
`TODO.md > ## In Progress` and nothing else ([Cycle-record](#cycle-record)). The `.vc-config.md`
`[validate]` table defines the commands that validate the work-repo.

### Cycles run on a bookmark

A cycle runs on one topic bookmark in the work-repo, created at the opening and named by the cycle
title's slug ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)). `main` advances only when
the finished cycle lands on it, so development is never done on `main`, a single-step cycle
included. The agent-repo needs no bookmark. Commands in [Cycle
bookmarks](agent-data/jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land), the long-lived case in [Long-lived
bookmarks][llb].

### Cycle shape

Single-step or multi-step is decided at the opening and fixed by the cycle's first push, with the
one coordinated exception below ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#cycle-shape)). Before that push the
In Progress block may be rewritten to either shape. After it:

- A single-step cycle is one commit, made by one push, carrying the opening's duties, the work, and
  the close-out's duties, titled with the bare cycle title in both repos. When the work turns out to
  need more steps, two choices, since the bookmark is still a draft:
  - land the commit as it is and run the additional work as one or more further cycles
  - turn the commit into the opening: amend its version-of-record to the `-0` form, re-title it with
    " opening" as a coordinated re-describe that keeps the `ochid:` trailer ([No re-describe without
    coordinating](agent-data/jj.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer)), and
    complete the cycle as multi-step.
- A multi-step cycle is a ladder and lands as a trapezoid or kept separate, never squashed: every
  rung's `ochid:` trailer is a change id, and a squash discards all but one. A ladder that shrinks
  to one rung still closes as a ladder, since its opening already pushed.

### Unplanned work

Work that arrives while a cycle runs goes one of two ways, and the user picks which
([why](agent-data/rationale.md#unplanned-work)):

- A rung inserted into the ladder, usually when it is inside the cycle's subject or blocks it.
- A `## Todo` or `## Waiting` entry, run as its own cycle later.

A rung inserted while the working copy already holds the next rung's edits sets those edits aside
as a patch first, so the inserted rung's commit carries its own change alone, and they return once
it has pushed.

### Cycle-record

A cycle's record is its `TODO.md > ## In Progress` block and nothing else, the cycle-record
([why](agent-data/rationale.md#cycle-record)).

- Items: title, problem, solution, acceptance check, deliberation, and the ladder heading its rung
  subsections, all provisional until close-out ([The In Progress
  block](agent-data/notes.md#the-in-progress-block)).
- Life: written at the opening, revised as rungs land, finalized by the closing commit, which moves
  it whole to `## Closed` (a single-step cycle's one commit writes it there directly), deleted by
  the next opening.
  - `## In Progress` reads `_No cycle currently in progress._` between cycles.
  - The closing commit's tree carries the final form, and the file never grows.
- After that jj holds it: `git log --grep "<cycle title>"` finds the commits, on the title the
  pushed bookends carry when a rename came mid-cycle, and the landmark on `main` (the trapezoid
  merge, or the single-step commit) holds the finished block in its `TODO.md > ## Closed`.
- No backfill: a rung carries no `[[N]]` placeholder, no SHA, and no version.
- Never amended: a late finding about a closed cycle is recorded where it is found, citing the
  landmark.
- Design findings that must outlive the cycle go into a `notes/` file by the rung that made them,
  never left in the block.
- Frozen history: `notes/chores/` and `notes/done.md` are never appended, still linked.

### Opening

The cycle's first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle starts at its first commit, which
then carries steps 1 and 2). A single-step cycle does all of it in its one commit, after steps 1
and 2 ([Cycle shape](#cycle-shape)). Before that commit ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#opening)):

1. Sync: sync both repos ([Sync](#sync)), whatever the cycle's form.
2. Bookmark: create and publish the cycle's bookmark, a push that needs approval.
3. Waiting: check each `## Waiting` entry's condition, and promote what is met into `## Todo` at
   the rank it names.
4. In Progress block: delete whatever `## Closed` holds, then move the chosen `## Todo` entry into
   `## In Progress`, shaped as [The In Progress block](agent-data/notes.md#the-in-progress-block)
   says, the specimen in [cycle-model.md](agent-data/cycle-model.md).
5. Bump: bump the version-of-record to the opening's version ([Suffix
   scheme](agent-data/versioning.md#suffix-scheme)), and the agent-files version with it when the
   cycle is an `agent-files` proposal ([Agent-files
   version](agent-data/versioning.md#agent-files-version)).
6. Rename: when the built artifact has consumers, rename `<name>` to `<name>-dev` ([Dev artifact
   name](agent-data/versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)). Land restores it.

Rungs are named, not numbered ([Steps are named, not numbered][snn]), and a multi-step cycle's
bookends are the cycle title plus " opening" and " closing" ([Cycle bookend titles][cbt]).

### The per-rung flow

Every commit (opening, each rung between, closing) goes through these steps, read from here
immediately before acting ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#the-per-rung-flow)):

0. Sync: sync both repos ([Sync](#sync)), required at the opening and the closing, optional
   between, the agent's or the user's call.
1. Mark current: mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
2. Bump: bump the version-of-record to this commit's version ([Suffix
   scheme](agent-data/versioning.md#suffix-scheme)), the agent-files version beside it in an
   `agent-files` proposal cycle.
3. Work: do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop ([Stop and
   ask](#stop-and-ask)).
4. Rung subsection: write what this rung changed, conceptually, into its subsection under the
   ladder. The rung stays `(current)` until step 7.
5. Validate: `vc-x1 validate` before every review, doc-only commits included. The full run rewrites
   files (`cargo fmt`), so use `--fast` while a review iterates. A failure is read and its cause
   named before validation runs again, and a failure that does not repeat is a finding, reported
   and given a Todo entry.
6. Work review: stop before writing any description and say "please review", as its own message with
   no title or body. Iterate until the user says "continue" / "go". The review is of the
   working-copy diff ([jj basics](agent-data/jj.md#jj-basics)).
7. Flip and describe: flip `(current)` to `(done)` the moment "done" is true, then write the
   description in [Commit-body form](agent-data/prose.md#commit-body-form), read from the file first
   with its specimen, [commit-model.md](agent-data/commit-model.md) ([Commit
   description](#commit-description)).
8. Description review: show the title + body and stop. Ask permission to commit and push without
   spelling out the invocation. The go covers the push only when it says so.
9. Commit + push: on the go, `vc-x1 commit -s b --title "..." --body "..."`, the commit and its
   push in one invocation ([Committing vs pushing](#committing-vs-pushing)), then [At
   rest](#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push).

### Committing vs pushing

A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`, never pre-committed with `jj commit`
([why](agent-data/rationale.md#committing-vs-pushing)). "Commit", "push",
and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit` is asked for by name and is for local
saves and [local ladder](#local-ladders) intermediates. What push does is in [vc-x1 push][vpush].

### Commit description

The title is a Conventional Commit, distinct within its cycle ([Commit titles and
descriptions][cdd]).
The body is in [Commit-body form](agent-data/prose.md#commit-body-form): no version, file list, or
deliberation ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#commit-description)).

### Pushing

Pushing is by `vc-x1 push`. The bookmark moves (create, land, trapezoid) use `jj git push` as jj.md
names, until vc-x1 owns them.

#### Before any push

([why](agent-data/rationale.md#before-any-push))

- This specific push has the user's explicit approval, or an explicit waiver covers it.
- Validation ran, and passed, after the last edit.

#### At rest: push, stop, squash-push

The contract that keeps both repos clean, the rule **Hard stop after the final push** its first
item's tail ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push)):

1. The agent publishes: completing a step means issuing its publishing command. The agent says what
   is worth saying *before* the final publishing command, responds with the one word "Published",
   and does nothing further until the user speaks.
2. The user squash-pushes: `vc-x1 squash-push -s a` whenever they want both repos fully pushed.

"Clean" means both repos' `@` empty. A late work-repo tweak after the push is a remote rewrite and
takes approval like any push ([vc-x1 push][vpush]).

### Close-out

The cycle's last commit is bookkeeping and its body describes that bookkeeping. A single-step cycle
does all of it in its one commit, step 5 aside ([Cycle shape](#cycle-shape)):

1. Acceptance check: run the check the opening stated and record pass or fail. A failure is a
   finding, and why it failed is determined.
2. Finalize the cycle-record in place ([Cycle-record](#cycle-record)):
   - sync the title if the scope shifted, and every anchor back-reference with it. A pushed rung
     title and the bookend pair keep their names, since retitling one is a re-describe of a
     published commit, so a rename mid-cycle reaches the block's text and the unpushed rungs only
   - replace the provisional solution statement with what was done
   - add the design subsections the deliberation grew
   - complete the closing rung's subsection
   - ask what in the block must outlive the cycle, and write it into the `notes/` file it
     belongs to
   - move the block whole to `## Closed`, leaving `## In Progress` reading
     `_No cycle currently in progress._`.
3. Validate: full validation, and update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
4. Size: when an agent-file changed, record the line count in `notes/agent-files-size.md`,
   smaller being the quasi-goal. A cycle that touched none adds no row.
5. Close-out shape ([Close-out shapes](agent-data/jj.md#close-out-shapes)):
   - choose with the user: trapezoid (the default) or keep separate
   - record the choice in the closing rung's subsection
   - reshape nothing yet, Land does.
6. Land: on the user's go, sync ([Sync](#sync)), restore the plain name, reshape per the choice,
   fast-forward `main`, install the artifact, delete the bookmark locally and remotely ([Bookmark
   per cycle](#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark),

7. Restart: the user restarts the agent, and before the exit anything the next agent needs is
   written into `TODO.md > ## Continuation notes`, the first section, which the next acquaint reads
   first, files or keeps, and resets ([Todo format](agent-data/notes.md#todo-format)).

## Working practices

([why](agent-data/rationale.md#working-practices))

- One command per invocation: no bundled steps (`a && b; c`), except a genuine pipeline or a tight
  pair where the join is the point.
- Exit status: never mask a command's exit status. The command under test runs bare and last in
  its invocation, since the Bash tool reports a nonzero exit, with `set -o pipefail` first when it
  is piped. No `&&` after a piped stage, no trailing `; echo "exit=$?"`. To report and still fail:
  `cmd || { rc=$?; echo failed=$rc; exit $rc; }`.
- Hooks: the Claude Code hooks are in `agent-data/` and `bash agent-data/hooks.sh install`, the
  user's to run, puts them in `~/.claude/hooks/` and registers them in `~/.claude/settings.json`.
  `bash-guard.sh` denies the two masks it can see, an echo of `$?` or `PIPESTATUS` and a `cargo`
  or `vc-x1` command piped into `tail`, `head`, `grep`, or `rg` without `pipefail`. `bash-allow.sh`
  skips the prompt for `cargo`, `jj`, and `vc-x1`, and `inhibit-sleep.sh` keeps the machine awake
  while a session works.
- Scratch files: repo-local `tmp/` (gitignored, `mkdir -p tmp` on demand). `/tmp` is for
  out-of-project temporaries.
- Slice reads: read the slice you need from long notes files. The acquaint read is `TODO.md`
  `offset=0, limit=60` ([notes.md](agent-data/notes.md#file-reads-read-the-slice-you-need)).
- https remotes: use https remotes, and check for an ssh remote first when a push dies at the
  network leg. A remote URL change needs the user's go.
- Delegate: mechanical subtasks go to lesser models (Opus/Haiku/Sonnet).
- No memory directory: `~/.claude/projects/<path>/memory/` is unused, the agent-files are.
- Speculation: mark it in durable text with "We think ..." ([Speculation
  marker](agent-data/prose.md#speculation-marker)).
- Plain synopsis: end a technical explanation in conversation with one, marked "The plain version:"
  ([Plain synopsis](agent-data/prose.md#plain-synopsis-after-technical-explanations)).

### A session's rules are its own agent-files

A session's rules are the agent-files of the project it started in, and its `custom.md`, and rules
living in any other repo are ignored unless these files or the user direct otherwise
([why](agent-data/rationale.md#a-sessions-rules-are-its-own-agent-files)). So another repo's own
protocol (a shared store's README, another project's agent-files) governs a write to it only as
far as the delegation reaches, and this file's conduct rules, the step reads, the reviews, the
per-push approval, and the stops, bind every commit and push the session makes, in any repo,
cycle or not. A repo with a live agent of its own is not written at all: message its agent.

### Stop and ask

Stop and ask on ambiguous input, on any deviation from the agreed plan, and when 5+ minutes on a
simple task has produced no progress ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#stop-and-ask)).

## Changing the agent-files

The template repository's payload is the copy adopters start from, and every adopter carries its
own copy ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#changing-the-agent-files)).

- Local experiments: a local agent-file may hold an unagreed experiment, diffed against the payload
  while the rules are being tried. After the experiment there may be a proposal.
- Proposing: a proposal is one set of diffs, to the rules or beyond them, that an adopter may or
  may not accept as is.
- Convergence: the adopter reviews the diff between the proposal and its files and accepts it as is
  or proposes changes. It is a negotiation whose goal is everyone accepting the same thing, and
  that goal is not a requirement.
- Acceptance: the adopter and the proposer agree on the contents, identical or not.
- Retirement: a resolved experiment retires like a finished Todo, adopted and rejected alike: the
  cycle that resolved it is its record.

## custom.md

When a `custom.md` exists at the workspace root, the agent must read it first, and it overrides
anything in the agent-files ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#custommd)). It is the place for what is
local to the workspace, one machine's paths and permissions, since a change every clone needs is a
cycle on the agent-file it belongs in. The session lock,
[session-lock.md](agent-data/session-lock.md), is an experiment it may carry.

You're right about the agent-repo, and I need to correct what I said last time.

**Rewinding the agent-repo**

With the agent gone after `/exit`, nothing is writing, so a rewind is safe from the concurrency side. My claim that "the conversation comes back in the next commit" holds only while the session runs and the transcript files keep their full content on disk. A rewind after `/exit` that checks out the older tree truncates those files, because the agent-repo is the live `~/.claude/projects/...` directory through the symlink. A restart then resumes from the shorter transcript. So it works, and it really does remove that part of the conversation. That makes it the one case where content the agent made is actually deleted. It should be a deliberate act with the agent stopped, never something an undo does as a side effect.

**`op --list` in `jj op log`'s style**

Your paste also shows the recording working: the `validate --fast` runs show up as runs. The look you like is a vertical list, one node per entry, a header line with an id, a relative time and a duration, then indented detail. Here is a mock-up of the same history in that style, one node per run:

```
@  01a189588552  2 hours ago, lasted 34 milliseconds
│  vc-x1-dev validate --fast
│  work-repo: 1 snapshot
○  01a188581d51  7 hours ago, lasted 20 milliseconds
│  vc-x1-dev validate --fast
│  work-repo: 1 snapshot
○  01a18813bf0b  8 hours ago, lasted 24 milliseconds
│  vc-x1-dev install --profile dev
│  work-repo: 1 snapshot
┆  15 operations no vc-x1 run recorded, 18 to 19 hours ago
○  01a1859dd8a2  1 day ago, lasted 3 seconds
│  vc-x1-dev commit -s b --title 'feat: each vc-x1 write records its run in the op log'
│  work-repo: 4 operations, commit, point bookmark (2), push bookmark
┆  1,340 operations no vc-x1 run recorded, before 2026-10-28 20:04
```

And with `--ops`, each run's operations listed under it in jj's own words, newest first like jj:

```
○  01a1859dd8a2  1 day ago, lasted 3 seconds
│  vc-x1-dev commit -s b --title 'feat: each vc-x1 write records its run in the op log'
│  76236e91c9c1  work-repo  push bookmark feat-undo-takes-back-the-last-vc-x1-run to git remote origin
│  ab15ca659779  work-repo  point bookmark feat-undo-takes-back-the-last-vc-x1-run to commit c594f1c06ba1
│  8b4e6e507d81  work-repo  point bookmark feat-undo-takes-back-the-last-vc-x1-run to commit c594f1c06ba1
│  2a0c7259f1f8  work-repo  commit 4db0c2e1d6fb
```

What this changes from the table:
- **Untagged stretches are always shown, collapsed to one dotted line,** in their place in time. A short `-n` no longer looks like a bug, because you can see where the history goes. `-n` still counts runs only.

content.text:
Honestly, it's helpful less often than it looks. Its main reason was undo, and that's gone. What's left is modest but real.

**Where it has already helped**
- **Debugging vc-x1.** Today the run id showed that the two "point bookmark" operations came from one command, which made the redundant transaction an obvious bug rather than two separate events. It also showed that a clone's operations belong together, apart from the untagged workspace init. Without the tag, an operation like `commit 4db0c2e1…` doesn't say whether vc-x1, raw jj, or something else made it.
- **Recovery by hand.** Under "no undo", a person can still use `jj op restore` on work that is theirs alone and referenced by nothing. The tag answers the hard part of that: which operation was just before the command I regret.
- **Seeing what triggered a snapshot.** `validate --fast` snapshotting the working copy is visible now. Before, it was one of fifteen identical "snapshot working copy" lines.

**What it costs**
- **Noise.** Four extra lines per operation in `jj op log`, most of them on snapshots. `vc-x1-command` repeats the first word of `vc-x1-args`, and `vc-x1-run-format` means nothing to a person.
- **It's local.** It never leaves `.jj`, so it does nothing for the record, for another clone, or for anyone after this machine.

**My view**

Keep it. It's built, it's cheap at run time, and it's the only way to tell what a vc-x1 command actually did to a repo. That's mostly a developer's tool for working on vc-x1, and today showed that's worth having. If the noise bothers you, the easy trim is to drop `vc-x1-command`, which you can derive from the args, and fold the format number into the run line, leaving two lines per operation. I wouldn't decide that yet. Living with it for a few cycles will show whether anyone reads it outside of debugging.

The same question applies to `op --list` even more. Without undo, it's purely a debugging and audit view. If the attributes turn out to matter only when something goes wrong, `jj op log` might be enough and `op --list` could go after all.

The plain version: the `vc-x1-…` lines tell you which vc-x1 command made each jj operation. That already helped us find a bug today, and it would help anyone fixing a mistake by hand with `jj op restore`. It's not something you'd read every day, so I'd keep it, maybe trim it to two lines, and see over the next few cycles whether it earns its space.

content.text:
I checked what reads each attribute. The answers are mostly "nothing", which supports trimming.

**`vc-x1-command` and `vc-x1-args`**

They're not 1:1. `vc-x1-command` is the subcommand clap parsed (`commit`, `validate`, `install`). `vc-x1-args` is the whole command line, with the body left out. Every args value determines its command, but many args values share one command. So `vc-x1-command` adds nothing `vc-x1-args` doesn't already say, and args is more informative.

`vc-x1-command` was written for a program to read: undo would match runs by command, such as refusing `clone` and `init`, without parsing the command line. Nothing reads it today. `RunTag::from_attributes` parses it, but `op --list` uses only the run id and the args. With undo gone, it has no reader. Dropping it settles the consistency question: one attribute holds the command, and it's the full one.

One small inconsistency remains in args: its first word is the binary as invoked, `vc-x1`, `vc-x1-dev`, or a path like `target/debug/vc-x1`. That's useful, since it says which build ran, but it isn't normalized. I'd keep it as it is.

**`vc-x1-run`**

Its one job is exact grouping: which operations came from the same invocation. Args can't do that on its own. Your paste has two `vc-x1-dev validate --fast` runs with identical args, and back-to-back identical commands are common. Time and adjacency usually separate them, but not always.

Who needs exact grouping once `op` and undo are both gone? Only a person doing `jj op restore` by hand who needs the first operation of a command that ran twice in a row. That's rare. So I agree that it's low value. The honest case for keeping it is that it's the one field a future tool couldn't reconstruct. Args you can always read, but which invocation an operation belonged to is lost once it isn't recorded. Its timestamp prefix also gives the run's start time, but jj's own operation times cover that.

**`vc-x1-run-format`**

This only matters if a program parses the record. Drop `op` and nothing does, so it goes too.

**The minimal form**

If `op` goes, the record could shrink to one attribute, `vc-x1-args`, one line per operation in `jj op log`. Or two, if you want to keep exact grouping with `vc-x1-run`. The typed record (`RunKey`, `RunTag::from_attributes`, the format version) and `src/jj/op_history.rs` would go with `op`, since they exist to read it back.

I'd go with args alone. It's what you read, and a reader can be reintroduced if a real need for grouping ever turns up. The run ids recorded so far stay in the op log either way.

The plain version: `vc-x1-command` is just the first word of `vc-x1-args`, and nothing uses it. `vc-x1-run` only matters for telling apart two identical commands run back to back, which is rare. If `op` goes, keeping only `vc-x1-args` gives one readable line per operation and drops the rest.

content.text:
Yes. A jj operation attribute is just a key and a string, so one attribute can hold both:

```
○  99b820661b2e @ 7 hours ago, lasted 20 milliseconds
│  snapshot working copy
│  vc-x1-run: 01a188581d517db3 vc-x1-dev validate --fast
```

**The form**
- **Key:** `vc-x1-run`. It reads naturally ("this operation is part of vc-x1 run …") and avoids `vc-x1: … vc-x1-dev`, which reads twice.
- **Value:** the id, one space, then the command line as `vc-x1-args` holds it now, with the body left out and the title kept. The id never contains a space, so a reader splits at the first space with no ambiguity.
- **No format attribute.** If the shape ever changes, the key changes (`vc-x1-run2`), which is how old and new records would be told apart.

**How long the id needs to be**

The run id's first 12 hex digits are its start time in Unix milliseconds. `01a188581d51` is exactly that, with no random part. The 13th digit is always `7`, the UUID v7 version marker, and the random bits come after it. So:
- **12 digits** is a millisecond timestamp. Two vc-x1 processes would have to start in the same millisecond on one machine to collide, which is unlikely but possible, for example from a script.
- **16 digits** (`01a188581d517db3`) adds 12 random bits. A collision needs the same millisecond and a 1-in-4,096 chance.
- **32 digits** is today's full id, and long for a line meant to be read.

I'd use 16, which keeps the line short, sortable by time, and safe for practical purposes. We could drop the UUID v7 layout and generate exactly "milliseconds plus 16 random bits" instead. That's simpler to explain, but the v7 code already exists and is tested.

**What changes**
- Each operation goes from four attribute lines to one.
- The typed record collapses to one key and a parse at the first space. With `op` gone, nothing reads it at all, so even the parse can wait for a reader.
- The records written so far keep their four-line form, since operations are never rewritten. They're all from this cycle's two days of `vc-x1-dev`, and nothing will read them.

This belongs to the current rung, which already changes the record's command line. Together with dropping `op`, the rung becomes something like **feat: a vc-x1 run is one line in the op log**: the combined attribute, the body left out, `op --list` and `op_history.rs` removed, and their tests replaced by a check that each operation carries the one line. Do you want it reshaped that way? That's a change to the agreed plan, so I'll wait for your go.

The plain version: yes. One attribute, `vc-x1-run: <16-digit id> <command line>`, says both which run the operation belongs to and what was run, on one line in `jj op log`. Sixteen digits is enough: the first twelve are the start time, and the last four add some randomness.

content.text:
That works, and it's better than the run id for what we've found useful. It records which build did something, which the run id never did. With today's builds, `jj op log` would show:

```
○  99b820661b2e @ 7 hours ago, lasted 20 milliseconds
│  snapshot working copy
│  vc-x1-run: vc-x1-dev 0.85.16-2+c594f1c06ba1.dirty validate --fast
○  2a0c7259f1f8 @ default@ 1 day ago, lasted 29 milliseconds
│  commit 4db0c2e1d6fb7292a5e70406ea98a932327d49cf
│  vc-x1-run: vc-x1-dev 0.85.16-2+c594f1c06ba1.dirty commit -s b --title 'feat: each vc-x1 write records its run in the op log'
```

**What it gains**
- **Which build made the operation.** The redundant "point bookmark" bug, for example, would be pinned to the build that has it, and a fix would show up as a later version no longer doing it. The version and commit already exist at compile time; the banner prints the same string, `.dirty` included.
- **A normalized app name.** Use the basename of what was invoked, `vc-x1` or `vc-x1-dev`, never a path like `target/debug/vc-x1`. That fixes the inconsistency in today's args.
- **One line per operation,** read by people, parsed by nothing.

**What it drops**
- **Exact grouping.** Two identical commands back to back can be told apart only by time. You've decided that's acceptable. If grouping is ever needed, an id could go under a new key then.

**Details**
- **Key:** I'd keep `vc-x1-run`. It reads as "the vc-x1 run that made this", and a key of `vc-x1` would read `vc-x1: vc-x1-dev …`.
- **Parameters:** the rules the rung already has. `--body` is left out, `--title` is kept, and any other value with a newline or over 100 characters becomes `<N chars>`.

**What goes away with it**

`RunId` and its UUID v7 code, the typed record (`RunKey`, `RunTag::from_attributes`, the format version), `op --list`, `src/jj/op_history.rs`, and their tests. What's left is one string built once per process and one `set_attribute` call per transaction, plus a test that each operation carries it.

So the reshaped rung would be roughly **feat: a vc-x1 run is one line in the op log**: the single attribute in this form, with `op` and its reader removed. It's a change to the agreed plan, so I'll wait for your go before reshaping the rung and its record. The cycle's ending, dead end or rescope, is still open after that.

The plain version: one line, `vc-x1-run: vc-x1-dev 0.85.16-2+c594f1c0… validate --fast`, says which program and which exact build ran which command. That's more useful than the run id, and everything built to read the old four-line record, including `op --list`, can go.

The attribute can't be keyless, but jj's own key solves it. jj-cli records its command line on every operation under `args`. The exit status 3 above is only from `rg -m` stopping the read early; the matches are complete:

```
○  e66ff4213525 wink@3900x default@ 1 day ago, lasted 26 milliseconds
│  snapshot working copy
│  args: jj diff --stat
```

If vc-x1 writes the same key, the two look alike in `jj op log`:

```
○  99b820661b2e @ 7 hours ago, lasted 20 milliseconds
│  snapshot working copy
│  args: vc-x1-dev 0.85.16-2+c594f1c06ba1.dirty validate --fast
○  e66ff4213525 wink@3900x default@ 1 day ago, lasted 26 milliseconds
│  snapshot working copy
│  args: jj diff --stat
```

**Why `args`**
- **No vc-x1 key at all.** The first word of the value says which program ran, `jj`, `vc-x1`, or `vc-x1-dev`, the same way for every operation.
- **It's jj's own convention, not a new one.** jj-lib's metadata map has room for it, and jj-cli fills it the same way.
- **The only difference from jj's form is the version after the program name.** jj doesn't record its own version, and ours is the useful part.

**The other ways to drop the key**
- **An empty key:** jj-lib would accept it, but `jj op log` would print `: vc-x1-dev …`.
- **Appending to the operation's description,** for example `commit 4db0c2e1… by vc-x1-dev 0.85.16-2+… commit -s b …`: vc-x1 controls those descriptions, so it's possible. But the description is jj's place for what the operation did, and a long command line would push that out of sight.

I'd go with `args`.

- **The record** becomes one attribute, `args: <app name> <version+commit> <parameters>`. The app name is the basename of what was invoked, and the parameters follow the rung's existing rules (body left out, title kept).
- **Removed:** `op --list`, `src/jj/op_history.rs`, `RunId`, and the typed record, with their tests.
- **One new test:** each operation a vc-x1 run makes, in every repo, carries the line.
- **The rung is retitled** to something like **feat: each vc-x1 operation records its command line**, with the subsection and Solution rewritten to match.

The plain version: `jj op log` already shows `args: jj diff --stat` for jj's own operations. If vc-x1 writes `args: vc-x1-dev 0.85.16-2+c594f1c0… validate --fast` the same way, there's no vc-x1-specific label at all, just the command line, whichever program ran it.

content.text:
Either works, and it's one constant in the code. I'd still pick `args`:

- **It matches jj.** jj's own operations already read `args: jj diff --stat`. With `args`, every operation in `jj op log` has the same line, and only the first word says which program ran. Anything that later reads command lines from the op log, a jj template or a script, finds jj's and vc-x1's under one key.
- **The version is the one difference.** Our value has the version after the program name and jj's doesn't. `app:` fits that better: the line says which app and build made the operation, then what it was asked to do.

So it's consistency with jj (`args`) against describing our line more exactly (`app`). I lean `args`, because one key across all operations is worth more than the slightly better label. Which do you want? I'll write the module with that key.

62	## In Progress
63	
64	### feat: undo takes back the last vc-x1 run
65	
66	Picked from `## Todo` as **undo takes back the last operation** (wink + agent, 2026-10-28), at the
67	opening of **push refuses rewriting the work trunk**, which this opening first carried and gave up
68	for this, wink's call (2026-10-28): undo is the safety net the push and squash rules lean on, so it
69	comes first. Run in the v0.3.1 form, wink's call (2026-10-28): every cycle from now on.
70	
71	#### Problem
72	
73	A vc-x1 write is local and so can be taken back, but only by raw jj, `jj op restore` in each repo,
74	two op logs for `-s b`, the agent-repo's moving with every session write. A `squash-push -s b` that
75	folds hours of uncommitted work into `@-` by mistake and pushes it leaves the work recoverable from
76	the op log and the remote rewritten, and getting both back means finding the right operation in each
77	repo by hand, restoring without clobbering the files on disk, and pushing the bookmark back past a
78	lease that the restore has made stale.
79	
80	#### Solution
81	
82	- Each vc-x1 run records itself in the op log jj already keeps, with no state file to disagree
83	  with it:
84	  - a run is one vc-x1 invocation, and a write is a run that commits an operation other than a
85	    working-copy snapshot or a git import, the operations nearly every run makes first
86	  - every operation a run commits carries the run's record as operation attributes,
87	    `Transaction::set_attribute`, the map jj-cli keeps its own `args` in, so `jj op log` shows them
88	  - the record is typed on our side, the map being strings: its keys an enum, its id a 128-bit
89	    `RunId` in the UUID v7 layout, its command the subcommand clap parsed, its command line for
90	    people with the body left out, and a format version
91	  - they are set where each transaction starts: `Session::start_tx` and the three that start their
92	    own, the working-copy snapshot and the git HEAD and git refs imports.
93	- `op --list -s w|a|b|p` shows the op log by run, `--list` an action flag as on `undo` and `-s`
94	  required as on the write commands, read with jj-lib (`op_walk::walk_ancestors` and each
95	  operation's metadata), the display ours since jj's templates and graph are jj-cli's:
96	  - a table under a header naming its columns, a row per run, newest first: RUN its id, STARTED,
97	    KIND `write` or `snapshot` for a run that only snapshotted, a count column per scoped repo,
98	    WORK, AGENT, or REPO, `-` where the run made none, and COMMAND, so `-s b` shows a run that
99	    touched both repos as one row
100	  - `--ops` shows everything: each row's operations under it, and each stretch of operations no
101	    run recorded, raw jj commands and operations from before the recording, as a row of its own,
102	    KIND `no run`
103	  - `-n/--runs N` counts runs alone, the stretches before and between them shown with them
104	  - read-only, with no snapshot, so looking at the log adds nothing to it
105	  - its walk and grouping are the ones `undo --list` uses, which adds each run's pushes, found by
106	    comparing the remote-tracking bookmarks before and after it.
107	- `undo --list -s w|a|b|p` shows what undo can take, a run being the unit, so a `commit --closing

content.text:
Yes, we agree, and option A does exactly that. I think "dead end" made it sound like the work gets thrown away. It doesn't.

**What lands on `main` under A**
- **The enhanced logging:** rungs p1 and p2. Every vc-x1 operation carries `args: vc-x1 <version+commit> <arguments>` in both repos.
- **No `undo`:** the undo rungs come off the ladder, and nothing of them was built.
- **No `op`:** it's already gone in this rung. It was built and removed, so it never reaches `main`.

v0.3.1 defines a dead-end closing as one that "keeps what is worth keeping, reverts the rest, and records what was tried, why it stopped, and what replaces it, then lands as a trapezoid like any closing". The word refers to the cycle's goal, undo, not to its commits. Here there's nothing to revert. The closing just records that undo stopped, and the logging lands as planned.

#### Solution

- Each vc-x1 run records itself in the op log jj already keeps, with no state file to disagree
  with it:
  - a run is one vc-x1 invocation, and a write is a run that commits an operation other than a
    working-copy snapshot or a git import, the operations nearly every run makes first
  - every operation a run commits carries one attribute, `args`, the key jj-cli keeps its own
    command line in, set by jj-lib's `Transaction::set_attribute`, so `jj op log` shows `args:
    vc-x1-dev 0.85.16-2+c594f1c06ba1 validate --fast` beside `args: jj diff --stat`
  - its value is the banner's program and build, then the arguments, the body left out and the
    title kept
  - it is set where each transaction starts: `Session::start_tx` and the three that start their
    own, the working-copy snapshot and the git HEAD and git refs imports.
- `jj op log` is the view of it: vc-x1 adds no reader of its own.
- `undo --list -s w|a|b|p` shows what undo can take, a run being the unit, so a `commit --closing
  --land` is one line however many operations it made:
  - a line per write, newest first: its id, when it ran, its command, the repos it touched with
    each one's operation count, and what it pushed, `main` from O to N or a bookmark deleted at O
  - a run that also acted outside the repos, an install or files init wrote, is flagged, since undo
    reaches the repos alone
  - `--ops` lists the operations under each line, `-v` being the global verbose flag already.
- `undo -s w|a|b|p` takes back the last write in the scoped repos, `-s b` both together, its
  operations in every repo as one unit:
  - the commits and bookmarks the write changed are reverted, the way `jj op revert` does it, a
    three-way merge of the state after the write's last operation back to the state before its
    first, onto the current one, so the named-run case below reuses it
  - the working copy keeps what is on disk now, `@` made to hold it, so an edit after the write and
    the agent journal the session keeps appending to are never cut back
  - an operation after the write other than a working-copy snapshot, another vc-x1 write or a raw
    jj command, is refused and named, since undoing the write would undo it too.
- undo rolls back what the write pushed: each remote bookmark it moved, from O to N, is shown and
  asked for, then pushed back to O with the lease at N, so a remote someone moved since is reported
  rather than overwritten, and one it deleted is recreated at O, the lease that it is still absent.
- `undo --run <id>` takes back an earlier write, later writes kept, when what followed is
  independent of it:
  - the id is the one `undo --list` shows
  - the revert is computed without being committed, and a result with a conflicted bookmark, a
    divergent change, or a remote bookmark moved since the write is refused, what tangled named
  - a clean result is shown and asked for, its push-backs as above.
- One undo per write: a redo is later, the attributes carrying it.
- The help, the README, and the agent-files name undo as how a mistake is taken back.

#### Acceptance check

`cargo test` passes with tests that:

- every write command's operations carry the run's one `args` line, in each repo it touches
- `undo --list` shows a `commit --closing --land` as one write with both repos' counts and its
  pushes, leaves out snapshot-only runs and raw jj commands, and with `--ops` lists the operations
- the mistake: hours of work in the work `@`, `squash-push -s b`, then `undo -s b` puts the work back
  in `@`, `@-` as it was, and the work bookmark on `origin` back at O, and an agent journal written
  in between survives
- `undo -s w`, `-s a`, and `-s p` take back their own repo's run alone
- an operation after the run is refused and named, a declined push-back leaves the remote as it is,
  and a remote moved since the run fails its lease and is reported
- `undo --run` takes back an earlier write with an independent write after it, the later one kept,
  and refuses one whose later writes built on it or moved its bookmark, naming them.

#### Deliberation

    title kept

    own, the working-copy snapshot and the git HEAD and git refs imports.

content.text:
`jj log` and `jj op log` draw two different graphs, and the first `@` means something different in each. On top of that, a second `@` appears inside our op-log lines.

**Two graphs**
- **`jj log` draws commits.** Each node is a commit, and `@` marks the working-copy commit: `olvutzls … ed6c454d`, the uncommitted work you're reviewing.
- **`jj op log` draws operations.** Each node is one change to the repo as a whole: a snapshot, a commit, a bookmark move, a push. Each operation records the full repo state at that moment: every commit, every bookmark, and where the working copy is. `@` marks the current operation, the newest state the repo is in. Other operations are `○`.

**The 12-digit value**

`ee0aa60c8b49` is an operation id. It's a separate id space from commit ids (`ed6c454d`) and change ids (`olvutzls`), so nothing in `jj log` will match it. The two connect by time travel: `jj log --at-op ee0aa60c8b49` shows the commit graph as it was at that operation, and `jj op show ee0aa60c8b49` shows what that operation changed.

**The second `@`**

```
@  ee0aa60c8b49 @ 11 minutes ago, …
○  862268e5f481 wink@3900x default@ 43 minutes ago, …
```

- **The first `@`** is the graph marker for the current operation.
- **The `@` after the id** is the user@host field, empty. vc-x1 records no user or host, so all that's left is the `@`. Raw jj fills it in, `wink@3900x`, and adds the workspace, `default@`.

That's the gap the Todo **vc-x1 stamps no user, host, or workspace on its operations** covers. Once fixed, our lines would read `wink@3900x default@` like jj's, and the stray `@` would go.

These operations still show the four `vc-x1-…` keys because the installed `vc-x1-dev` is the previous build. The one-line `args` record is only in the working copy. Installing it with `vc-x1 install --profile dev` would make the next operations show `args: vc-x1-dev 0.85.16-2+… …`.

The plain version: in `jj op log`, the leading `@` means "the repo's current state", and the 12-digit value is an operation id, not a commit, so it never shows up in `jj log`. The `@` after the id is an empty user@host, because vc-x1 doesn't fill in your username and machine yet.

# Commit model

Two commit bodies from the `config loader` cycle in [cycle-model.md](cycle-model.md), shown as
specimens rather than a skeleton: a work rung's body and a bookend's. Copy the shape, not the
words. The rules are in [Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form).

## A work rung

Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`

```
Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config::loader` finds and reads the file and returns the text with
    its path, so a caller that only wants to know which file was read
    stops there.
  - `config::parser` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands
    it a string and never touches the filesystem.
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field
    access moves behind the module boundary and the CLI no longer knows
    the file's shape.
```

The intro states this commit's problem and defines "split", the word the title assumes. Each `*`
is one facet of it, each `-` under a `*` answers that facet, and nothing names a file that the
diff already lists.

## A bookend

Title: `refactor: extract config loader opening`

```
Opens the cycle "refactor: extract config loader". Its record is the
In Progress block in TODO.md.
```

A bookend resolves no problem of its own, so its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the
cycle by its title and pointing at its record. The closing's body is the same shape with "Closes".

132:### Commit-body form
133-
134-The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
135-shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
136-problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
137-bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
138-statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.
139-
140-- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
141-  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
142-  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
143-  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
144-  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
145-- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
146-  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
147-  to be more than one commit.
148-- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
149-  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
150-  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.
151-- **One facet is the trivial commit**: the intro, one `*`, one or more `-` under it. Not a second
152-  form, the general form at its smallest.
153-- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
154-  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
155-  the In Progress block. No `*`, no `-`.
156-
157-**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution, and the
158-pairing is what a reader counts on: the `-` answers the `*` above it, with no rule to consult. The
159-typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds every facet, `^ - ` every solution). Bodies are
160-read as plain text, in `jj log` and in terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever
161-flattens them the indentation still carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and
162-a linter's consistent-marker rule is wrong to normalize them.

│
~  A vc-x1 run leaves operations in each repo's op log that nothing ties
   to the run or to vc-x1: unlike jj's own, they carry no command line,
   and no hostname or username, so taking back what one run did means
   guessing which operations were its.

   carries a typed run record as operation attributes, a 128-bit id in
   the UUID v7 layout, the subcommand, the command line, and a format
   version, set at each of the four places a session starts a
   transaction, so `jj op log` shows which run made each one. See details
   in zDOING.md.

139:## Suffix scheme
140-
141-The cycle (opening -> commits -> closing, per the [Cycle protocol](../AGENTS.md#cycle-protocol))
142-encodes each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a
143-Preparation**.
144-
145-This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is not
146-a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries neither a
147-number nor a version (see [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)).
148-The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and nothing dereferences one.
149-
150-- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
151-- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: the commits between
152-- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)
153-
154-**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0` and
155-starts at `-1` (its first commit). A single-step cycle is one commit, the Close-out, and carries the
156-bare `X.Y.Z` ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
157-needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0`
158-step without renumbering siblings.
159-
160-Disambiguation:
161-
162-- `-10`: commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
163-- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).
164-
165-**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:
166-
167-- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle

vc-x1-dev 0.85.16-2+c594f1c06ba1.dirty

Commit the working copies as a rung's pair, one commit per repo of a
dual workspace, each stamped with the other's change id, and push it
in the same invocation, as `vc-x1 push` would.

The diff and the description are reviewed before the commit, so the
push publishes what was reviewed. --no-push keeps the commit local,
for a look at it by `vc-x1 show -s both @-` before `vc-x1 push`, and
`[commit] push = false` makes that the default, --push overriding it.

-r REV is the commit the description is for: `@` by default,
committed as the working copy, else `@-` or any draft below it,
described in place with no new commit and its trailer stamped, so a
commit made by hand becomes a rung's. A draft below `@-` is kept
local, since push publishes `@-`. Every argument is a flag: the old
positional is refused, naming -r.

--closing <BM|REV> closes the cycle whose tip it names, onto the trunk,
--land's or `[cycle] trunk`, `main` when absent: one commit above the
trunk is finalized in place, more get the closing commit, the merge of
the trunk and the tip. A tip that is not @- is closed by a detour, @
moving onto it and returning after. --land [TRUNK] lands it: the trunk
fast-forwarded and pushed and the closing's bookmark deleted, every
check first: the one named, or for a revision the current or nearest
parent bookmark above the trunk, several refused with the list.

-s is required: `b` makes both commits now, `w` the work half with
the agent half left to push, `a` the agent repo alone, unpaired, with
no trailer, and `p` a plain repo with no trailer. -R is optional and
says where. --body is the text, or @PATH to read it from a file.

Usage: vc-x1-dev commit [OPTIONS] --scope <SCOPE>

Options:
  -r, --revision <REV>
          The commit the description is for: `@` by default, committed as the
          working copy; `@-` or any draft below it is described in place with no
          new commit, its trailer stamped, so a commit made by hand becomes a
          rung's. Not with `--opening` or `--closing`

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

  -R, --repo <PATH>
          Where: a path in the workspace for `-s b|w`, its root or either repo,
          or the repo itself for `-s p` [default: the current directory]

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

  -s, --scope <SCOPE>
          Which repos, required: `w|work`, `a|agent`, `b|both`, or `p|por`
          
          [possible values: work, agent, both, por]

      --title <STR>
          Commit title, the Conventional Commit line; with `--opening` or
          `--closing` the bare cycle title [default with `--closing`: read from
          the opening]

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --body <STR|@PATH>
          Commit body, the problem and its solutions, or @PATH to read it from a
          file [default with `--closing`: `[closing] body`, or the opening's for
          a single-step cycle]

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --closing <BM|REV>
          Close the cycle whose tip this names, a bookmark or a revision, onto
          the trunk, `--land`'s or `[cycle] trunk`: one commit above it is
          finalized in place, more get the closing commit, the merge of the
          trunk and the tip

      --dead-end
          With `--closing`, close the cycle as a dead end: the title ends "
          dead-end closing", always on a closing commit

      --opening [<BOOKMARK>]
          Make the work commit the cycle's opening: " opening" is appended to
          the bare cycle title, and BOOKMARK is created at the work `@-` and
          pushed to `origin` [default: the bare title's slug]

      --skip <SIDE>
          With `--opening`, what it leaves out: `local`, the bookmark is already
          at the work `@-` and is pushed; `remote`, it is created and not
          pushed; `both`, it is only checked. With `--land`, which side of the
          cycle's bookmark is kept: `local`, `remote`, or `both`, none deleted

          Possible values:
          - local:  The bookmark exists at the work `@-` already, so it is not
            created, only pushed
          - remote: The bookmark is created and not pushed
          - both:   The bookmark exists and is neither created nor pushed

      --land [<TRUNK>]
          With `--closing`, land the cycle on TRUNK, the closing's first parent:
          fast-forward it to the closing, push it, and delete the cycle's
          bookmark [default: `[cycle] trunk`, else `main`]

      --bookmark <NAME>
          The bookmark to advance to the work commit, locally, any on the work
          commit's line, at or below it [default: the line's nearest, or
          `--opening`'s]

      --no-advance
          Leave the line's bookmark where it is, rather than advancing it to the
          work commit

      --push
          Push what was committed, over `[commit] push = false`

      --no-push
          Keep the commit local, over `[commit] push`, true when absent

      --dry-run
          Dry run: show what would be done without executing

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

file.content:
rebased: `jj rebase -b @ -d <b>`.
  - `@` already sits on `<b>`, or `<b>` isn't on `@-`'s line (diverged / `@` ahead) -> `@` is left
    untouched, with a note why.
- **Bot repo** (`.claude`): no-op when `@-` is already the `main` tip, so `@` keeps its change id
  and any live session writes stay in the working copy. When `main` moved, `jj new main` starts a
  fresh empty `@` on the new tip, and the prior `@` (e.g. `/exit`'s trailing session writes) is
  preserved as a sibling head. If `@-` isn't on `main`, `sync` errors rather than strand it.

On any failure during fetch/classify/act/reposition (conflicted rebase, subprocess error, anything)
`sync` **stops where the failing step stopped**. Nothing is auto-reverted, so the state can be
inspected as-is (jj's operation log holds everything, so nothing is lost by stopping). Before
acting, sync captures each repo's pre-sync `jj op` id in memory, and the failure report lists
every repo's op id. The undo is explicit, per repo: `jj op restore <op> -R <repo>`. Nothing
persists across
invocations: a snapshot that outlives its run is a stale target waiting to rewind unrelated work.
That is also why the former `revert` subcommand was removed at 0.78.3: it restored the persisted
snapshot with no guard against discarding operations recorded after the failed sync. A safer
revert would derive its target from the op log and refuse when unrelated operations sit in
between. Until such a design exists, `jj op log` + `jj op restore` is the recovery.

```
vc-x1 sync -s b                       # both repos of the dual workspace the cwd is in

content.content:
# Notes

This directory contains various notes and documentation related to the project. Each file is
organized by topic for easy reference.

The chores-NN.md files in [chores/](chores) and [done.md](done.md) are frozen history: the records
of cycles that closed before the cycle-record rule ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
Nothing is appended to them. They stay until the agent-repo transcripts are comfortable to read a
cycle from, then both retire in one cycle after a permalink sweep of the links into them (the `##
Waiting` entry in [../TODO.md](../TODO.md)). A cycle's live record is [../TODO.md](../TODO.md)'s `##
In Progress` block, and a closed cycle's is its `## Closed` block in the landmark commit's tree.

On trial since the cycle "feat: sync is safe by default" (2026-10-09), a cycle's record is kept in
[../zDOING.md](../zDOING.md) instead, the agent-files not yet saying so, and that cycle's landmark
holds its finished block there.

Tool architecture lives at the repo root in [`../ARCHITECTURE.md`](../ARCHITECTURE.md): the
CLI-args / `Context`+`Params` split, a generic module map, the subcommand model, and what the
Context+Params port and the options_flags extraction *are* (the *live status* is in the chores
files).

Multi-cycle programs too big for a TODO.md entry get their own dated plan file, e.g.
[refactor-20260716.md](refactor-20260716.md) (typed jj facade -> jj-lib in-process): one `##`
section per stage, so chores and todo entries can reference a stage by anchor. The plan file owns
the forward design, and chores still records each shipped cycle.

A rule that governs what the tool does, rather than a record of what was done, gets its own topic
file so it can be found without knowing which cycle produced it, e.g.
[jj-version-policy.md](jj-version-policy.md). The investigation behind such a rule stays where it
happened (a plan file or a chores section) and is linked from the policy, so neither restates the
vc-x1 list -r ..@ -n 3       # 2 descendants + @ (3 commits, @ at bottom)
vc-x1 list -r ..@.. -n 3     # 1 descendant, @, 1 ancestor (3 commits)
vc-x1 list -r ..@.. -n 4     # 1 descendant, @, 2 ancestors (4 commits)
```

### jj config and the new-file size limit

vc-x1 reads jj's config as `jj` does: the defaults, the user's (`~/.config/jj/config.toml`, or
`$JJ_CONFIG`), and the repo's own, which jj keeps under the user's config dir and `jj config set
--repo` writes.

A snapshot takes no new file over `snapshot.max-new-file-size`, 1 MiB by default. `jj` warns and
goes on without it, but in vc-x1 that is an error, at every subcommand that snapshots, push
included, before either repo commits, so nothing is committed without a word. The error
names each refused file and its size, and the fixes:

- add the file to `.gitignore`
- raise the limit for that repository only, `jj -R <repo> config set --repo
  snapshot.max-new-file-size <size>`
- in an agent-repo, whose files are its session transcripts, lift the limit there, `jj -R
  <agent-repo> config set --repo snapshot.max-new-file-size 0`, 0 meaning no limit

vc-x1 never sets the limit itself, since a repo's value overrides the one the user chose. A file
the limit refused stays out until one of these is done, and then the command is run again.

### Shell completion

vc-x1 never sets the limit itself, since a repo's value overrides the one the user chose. A file
the limit refused stays out until one of these is done, and then the command is run again.

### What vc-x1 records in jj's op log

Every operation a vc-x1 command commits, in every repo it touches, carries one attribute, `args`,
the key jj itself keeps its command line in, so `jj op log` shows which program made each operation
and with what:

```
○  5b27bdf2dba6 @ default@ 1 minute ago, lasted 30 milliseconds
│  commit 53373a7ee89e3c3f5b5ef86de7d688f9731fae12
│  args: vc-x1-dev 0.85.16-2+c594f1c06ba1.dirty commit -s b --title 'feat: ...'
○  862268e5f481 wink@3900x default@ 48 minutes ago, lasted 25 milliseconds
│  snapshot working copy
│  args: jj diff --stat --no-pager
```

- The value is the banner's program and build, the commit it was built from and `.dirty` when
  edits were compiled in, then the arguments.
- A commit's `--body` is left out, since the commit carries it, and its `--title` is kept. Any
  other value with a newline or over 100 characters is shown as its length, `<N chars>`.
- vc-x1 adds no view of its own: `jj op log` reads it, and `jj op restore` is the recovery by hand.

content.text:
The source didn't change. What changed is which commit it is. The id a build carries is the commit its source sits on, plus whether there were edits on top.

- **Before the closing:** `@-` was the last rung, `09aca74d`, and `@` held the closing's edits that weren't committed yet. That build was stamped `09aca74db42c.dirty`, meaning "this commit plus edits".
- **The closing commit** turned those edits into a commit of their own, `fbe48200`, and left `@` empty.
- **Your install:** the same files now are exactly `fbe48200`, so the build is stamped `fbe48200b7c8`, clean.

Two details in your output follow from that:
- **It recompiled (1.88 s) even though no source changed.** `build.rs` embeds the commit id as `VC_X1_COMMIT`, and cargo rebuilds when that value changes. That's the only difference between the two binaries.
- **The first line still says `09aca74db42c.dirty`.** That banner comes from the binary doing the install, which is the one I had installed. The new binary reports `fbe48200b7c8`, as your `-V` shows.

The plain version: same code, but before the closing it was "rung `09aca74d` plus edits" and after it's exactly "the closing `fbe48200`", so the build id changed from a dirty one to a clean one.
